sourceDesc.p: Traduction anglaise originale produite avec l'assistance d'un modele de langage (Claude, Anthropic), a partir du texte latin de zoo60/1l.xml (Conrad de Halberstadt, Liber similitudinum naturalium, Tractatus IV De animalibus, edition critique inedite d'Iolanda Ventura, these de doctorat 1999/2003, via la base Sourcencyme, IRHT), deja present dans le corpus Zoomathia. Traduction generee par IA, non relue par un specialiste : a verifier avant tout usage scientifique cite. Traduction complete : 136 chapitres (le prologue, tres court, est fusionne comme paragraphe d'ouverture du chapitre 1, pour que la numerotation des chapitres corresponde exactement a celle du temoin latin dans le graphe genere). Chaque chapitre regroupe plusieurs citations d'autorites anciennes et medievales (Aristote, Pline l'Ancien, Isidore de Seville, le Physiologus, le De naturis rerum, Ambroise, etc.) associant le comportement d'un animal a une lecon morale ; les references bibliques et patristiques abregees dans le texte source sont conservees telles quelles dans la traduction.

div.head: Prologue. Casting Off What Burdens
div.p: [Prologue] It remains now to set forth examples from the animals. These are distinguished thus: some are flying creatures, like birds; some are swimming creatures, like fish; some are creatures that walk, like beasts and beasts of burden; some are creeping creatures, like serpents and worms — from whose natures and properties much can usefully be applied to the conduct of men. And Job said meaningfully: 'Ask the beasts, and they will teach you; the birds of the air, and they will tell you; speak to the earth, and it will answer you; and the fish of the sea will declare it to you.' For all these teach us, speak to us, and answer us, when from considering them we perceive how we ought to order our necessary actions.

A man ought to cast away those things that weigh him down and hinder him, after the example of the eagle, which, according to Aristotle in Book VII of the Animals, sits upon its eggs for thirty days, and is greatly burdened in the nest, so that it cannot hunt; hence it is not able to feed more than two chicks, and therefore it casts away the third egg or the third chick.

div.head: Hiding in Time of Adversity
div.p: A man ought sometimes to hide himself in time of adversity, after the example of the turtledove. Which, as Aristotle says in Book VII of the Animals, lies hidden in winter — for no one, so to speak, has ever seen a turtledove in winter — and it begins its hiding while very fat.

Likewise the peahen, as the same author says in the same place, hides her eggs, lest they be broken by the peacock. The reason for this, according to Albert, is that he sometimes mates with the hen while she is sitting on the eggs, and so they are broken. But Pliny says that he breaks them out of desire to brood himself, while the Physiologus says it is out of envy, because he hates his own offspring. So too a man ought to hide his good works, lest they be corrupted by the devil through the display of vainglory. For the hen that clucks too loudly after laying an egg quickly loses it.

Likewise, according to the same author in the same place, tunny-fish hide and lie hidden in winter in the deep, and after their hiding become very fat; so too, in time of adversity, a man ought to lie hidden in the depth of humility, and then grow fat with the fatness of grace, and so on.

Likewise, one ought to hide oneself sometimes both in time of grace and of adversity and of prosperity. For, as Aristotle says in the same place, some fish lie hidden in summer, such as the glaucus and the gilthead, because at that time, especially under the Dog-star, they are caught on account of the disturbance of the sea; so too a man ought to hide himself even in time of prosperity, lest he then be caught by the devil.

Likewise, according to the Philosopher in Book VII of the Animals, stags, once they have shed their horns, lie hidden, since they lack weapons. And so the stag, fearing wolves, hides by day, but goes out to pasture by night; but once its horns have grown back, then it goes out safely, since it has weapons.

div.head: Abstinence
div.p: Abstinence is effective for putting off the oldness of evil habit. For, as the Physiologus says, the serpent, when it feels itself weighed down by old age, wishing to put off its old skin, fasts for forty days and nights, so that its skin may thereby more easily be loosened. So too a man wishing to be renewed, and to put off the old habit of carnal desire, must first abstain from food and delicacies. Leo, in a sermon: through the voluntary afflictions of abstinence, the flesh dies to its desires, and the spirit is renewed in virtues.

Likewise, the delights of gluttony are to be chastened by abstinence. For, as Pliny says in Book VIII, lions rarely drink, and feed only every other day, abstaining from food for three days at a time. Whence Gregory says: by this — that we abstain from what is lawful — the things we formerly committed unlawfully are pardoned in us.

Likewise, an example of abstinence is seen in the she-bear, which, as Aristotle says in Book VII, lies hidden for about forty days: during this time it is clear that they eat nothing, for if they are caught then, their stomach and intestines are found empty; but during the time of hiding, both male and female become very fat. So too with the body: when food is withdrawn, the soul grows fat.

Likewise, the Philosopher says in the second book of the Animals that the crocodile sees weakly in water, since water is thicker than air, but outside the water it sees very sharply; so too, in the waters of delights, a man sees little in contemplation, but outside them he sees better. Ecclesiasticus: I thought to withdraw my flesh from wine, that I might turn my mind to wisdom.

div.head: Sloth
div.p: Sloth. Ambrose, in the book of the Hexameron: the lazy ass, exposed to prey, teaches us that we ought to be more lively, and not grow sluggish in laziness of heart and mind, but take refuge in faith, which is accustomed to lighten heavy burdens.

Likewise, the cold of sloth and the heat of desire are especially harmful to the soul. An example of this is found in fish, which, as Aristotle says in Book VII, often die from heat near the surface, whence in summer they flee the warm shores for the deep sea; cold too is very harmful to them, especially to those that have a stone in their head, such as crabs — for such a stone easily freezes from the cold, and they die. So too a man ought to flee the heat of desire into the depth of the sea, that is, into the bitterness of tears; and to those who likewise have a stone in the head, that is, hardness of mind, the cold of sloth is harmful, because through it the heart is made harder still and brings on the death of despair.
Likewise, it is as with the serpent called the hypnale, of which Solinus says that its strike overtakes one as in sleep; so too sloth destroys through the sleep of laziness and inertia.

div.head: The Active Life
div.p: The active life. The active are like fish in the waters, in the tears of penitence and devotion; the contemplative are like the birds of the sea, through the elevation of contemplation.

Likewise, the active are like water-birds, which, according to Aristotle, have feet that are broad and closed, not divided between the toes, on account of the need for swimming; likewise short tails, lest in swimming they be hindered by the wetting of the tail. So too the active, whose task it is to relieve the needs of others through works of mercy, ought to have broad feet — that is, affections extended to all — and, without division or discord in their works, ought to have undivided toes; they ought also to have short tails, that is, swift dispatch of what must be done, giving without delay.

div.head: Flatterers
div.p: Flatterers are like certain sea-beasts, of which Jorach says that they breathe out water from their jaws together with a vapor full of fragrance, which scent other fish follow, entering into its jaws; and it at once swallows them and feeds upon them. So too flatterers and heretics draw in and swallow the simple with certain sweet words.

Likewise the same Jorach says there is a fish called 'faszez,' in whose mouth confined water becomes sweet, so that smaller fish follow it, and it catches and swallows them. So in the matter at hand: Proverbs 18: the deep words from the mouth of a man are like water.

Likewise, the sweet words of flatterers sometimes kill, but the harsh words of a friend bring back to life — just as the cicada, if drenched in oil, is killed by it, because, its pores being blocked, it cannot breathe; but if vinegar is at once poured over it, it revives, because this opens the pores that the force of the oil had closed.

div.head: Ambition
div.p: Ambition. Sometimes, while great dogs quarrel over a bone and, in the midst of it, let it fall, a little dog comes and, finding the bone, eats it; so too, when great men quarrel in the court over some vacant benefice or prelacy, it is sometimes taken from both the quarreling parties and given to some simple, good man who was not expecting it. Luke 20: he has put down the mighty from their seat, and exalted the humble.

div.head: A Friend Remains as Long as Usefulness Remains
div.p: A friend remains only as long as usefulness remains. An example of this we see in the hawk, which, as long as it is fit for the hunt, is loved by its master and carried on his hand; but when it is no longer fit for the hunt, it is no longer cared for, or, when it dies, it is treated as a carcass. So Seneca says: a friend who was taken up for the sake of usefulness remains and pleases only as long as he is useful.
Likewise, the cubs of foxes, when they find no milk in their mother's udders, bite her with their teeth and treat her as though she were a stranger.
Likewise, a dog loves a fleshy bone only as long as it finds something on it to gnaw; so too, and so on.

div.head: Love
div.p: Spiritual love draws upward, but carnal love draws downward, toward the earth and the lowest things. As a sign of this, the brute beasts, which seek and love only earthly things, have their heads bent down toward the earth, but man has his raised upward toward the heavens. Basil, in the Hexameron: all cattle are of the earth, and therefore bend down toward it, but the other planting, the heavenly one, differs from the brutes as much in dignity as it does in the manner of its form.

Likewise, spiritual love — in which the life of the soul consists — lasts and is preserved the longer, the less it has of the heat of earthly desire. For, as Pliny says in Book VII, the stag never suffers from fever, and lives a very long time — more than a hundred years; and this was discovered in the stags of Alexander, caught a hundred years after his death, which had gold rings placed in their nostrils by him. So too a man free from the fever of burning desire, in the charity that is the life of the soul, is preserved the longer.

Likewise, the fire of divine love does not lay waste the soul, but renews it. Whence such souls are like garments made from salamander-wool, since, as it is said in the book On the Natures of Things, Pope Alexander had a garment made from this creature, which, when it needed to be cleaned, was not washed with water, but was cast into the fire, and thus grew bright through the fire.

div.head: Spiritual Armor
div.p: The spiritual armor of men is likened to the natural armor of brute animals. For, as Pliny says in Book XI, nature has played with the weapons of the animals: to the stag it gave scattered antlers; lions have claws, wolves teeth, hares swiftness for fleeing, bees their stings. So too let the spiritual man live like the stag against the temptations of the flesh, with two horns — that is, with prayer against inward thoughts, and with fasting, by which the outward stirrings of the flesh are put to flight; he ought to help himself by cutting open and exposing what lies hidden within, through confession, grinding it down with the tooth, through contrition. Likewise, by fleeing the occasion of sin. Likewise, by pricking past sins with the sting, through satisfaction.

div.head: Avarice
div.p: They are likened to birds of prey, for Ambrose says, in the third book of the Hexameron, that hawks have no bond of companionship except the conjugal one, on account of their eagerness for plunder and their watchfulness for ambush; for avarice shuns the company of the many.

Likewise, as Aristotle says in Book VII, eagles feed their young until they can fly, and then cast them out of the nest and drive them from every place round about. They cast them out, needing this care, on account of envy — for they are envious toward all, and are of a violent hunger. So too the avaricious cast out their own household, lest they be obliged to spend on them; they envy everyone, always fearing lest something of theirs be lost, and are of a violent hunger for acquiring money.

Likewise, they are likened to griffins, of whom Solinus says, in chapter twenty-one: in Asiatic Scythia there are lands rich, yet uninhabitable; for though they abound in gold and gems, griffins — the fiercest of birds, raging beyond all frenzy — guard them entirely, and tear apart those who approach. Just as these birds do not turn these riches to their own use, so too the avaricious. Ecclesiasticus: he who loves riches shall gain no fruit from them.

div.head: Blasphemy
div.p: Blasphemy. Crows, as the book On the Natures of Things says, assail with their cawing the eagle and other noble birds, which they dare not touch; but when these have endured much, at last, overcome by impatience, they tear the troublesome crows to pieces. So too, some who blaspheme God and the saints and good men are, after long patience, torn apart by them in turn.

div.head: Flatterers (Blanditores)
div.p: Flatterers are likened to scorpions. Which, as Gregory says, advance by stroking, and do not bite from the front, but strike with the tail. The Gloss on the Apocalypse: the scorpion is flattering in face, but stings secretly with its tail.

div.head: Gratitude for Kindness Received
div.p: One must not forget kindness received, as the elephant teaches us, of which Solinus says that when it is first captured by a hunter, it is struck and afflicted with many blows.

Aristotle says the same thing in Book VII of the Animals: then another man comes, who wishes to have it obedient to himself; he approaches and frees it from the hand of the one striking it, and the elephant, perceiving this, grows gentle at his hands, and, recognizing him as its liberator, loves him and obeys him. So then, if a brute animal so loves its liberator, how much more should the soul love Christ. ... Do not forget to do good and to share.

div.head: Good Men, Likened to Bees
div.p: Good men are likened to bees. First, on account of cleanliness. Aristotle says in Book VIII: bees approach nothing rotten, nor do they use any food unless it has a sweet moisture; they love clear, pure, flowing waters, and make their honey only in a clean vessel. Likewise they carry their dead outside, so that their dwelling may be clean, and in the same way they cast out their waste. So too a good man ought to flee all the rot of sin, love the sweet moisture and food of grace, love the pure, clear, flowing waters of divine wisdom, and remove from the house of his heart not only what is dead — that is, mortal sins — but also what is superfluous — that is, venial sins.

Second, on account of prudence, for, as Aristotle says in Book VIII, they have a greater subtlety of understanding than many animals: they know when winter is coming, for then they do not go out from the hive; and the watchers among them also recognize coming rain. So they have prudence with respect to the seasons. So too a good man ought prudently to foresee the times and accommodate himself accordingly.

Second, they are prudent with respect to their works. Aristotle, in the same place: bees are assigned to different tasks. For some bring in flowers, others soften the wax, and others bring water; and in fair weather they work continually, when they have suitable conditions. So too every good man ought diligently to do what he can, and so on.

Third, with respect to obstacles: for, according to Aristotle in the same place, when the wind rises, they carry a small stone as ballast against the wind; so too a man ought to steady himself with good works against the wind of temptation.
Likewise it is said that they smear their hives with bitter juices against enemies; so too a man ought to fortify himself with the bitter tears of compunction against the enemy and his assaults.

Third, they are likened to bees on account of diligence in work, for, as Pliny says in Book XI, bees go out to their tasks and labors, and none lets a day pass idly when the sky permits; indeed, according to Aristotle in the same place, the hardworking ones fight against the idle and kill them, and especially their kings do this, and drive them out of the hive. Whence Pliny, in the same place: when the swarm goes out to its work, some gather flowers with their feet, others with their mouths and drops of dew, the young ones, growing the down of their whole body, go out to work, while the elders work within. So too good men ought above all to avoid idleness and press on unceasingly in good works, staying close by, and in their humility.

Fourth, as to obedience. Whence Ambrose, in the Hexameron: bees appoint themselves a king, not by chance, but by judgment; they love this king as one established by themselves; and bees that do not obey the laws of the king condemn themselves, as it were, to a self-imposed penance, so that they die of the wound of their own sting; and they defend their king with the utmost protection, and think it a fine thing to perish for him; nor does any bee dare to leave the hive or approach any pasture, unless the king has gone out first and claimed the flight as his own to lead. If this is so, consider how great a reverence and obedience religious men ought to have toward their superior.

div.head: Goodness Depends on Rest and Motion
div.p: Goodness depends greatly, at times, on rest and on motion. For domestic animals move less than wild ones, and are therefore of greater moistness than the wild, and so domestic meats are better for digestion: for from much rest the pores are closed and the heat is kept within, by which the coarse humors are consumed, and so the flesh becomes soft and refined; but because they eat and drink much, they grow fatter and nourish more. So too spiritual and contemplative men, who rest and dwell within themselves more than the active, are moistened more than the active through the compunction of tears, in whom, from much rest, the pores — that is, the outward senses — are closed, and the coarse humors in them — that is, of earthly thoughts and affections — are dissolved; whence they grow soft with piety and are refined by the scantness of food and drink; but because they abound inwardly in spiritual nourishment, they are filled with the fatness of consolation and grace. The Psalmist: let my soul be filled as with marrow and fatness.

div.head: Song
div.p: The song of divine praise delights the angels. An example of this is seen in dolphins, of which Solinus says that they are soothed by music, rejoice in the songs of pipes, and gather in schools wherever there is harmony; so too the angels delight in the voice of those who sing and praise God. Whence Basil says, in the Hexameron, that psalm-singing puts demons to flight and invites the angels to the aid of salvation.

Likewise, it lightens the tedium of this life, for Ambrose says that the nightingale — that is, the philomel, a wakeful guardian — while she warms her eggs in the fold of her body, consoles the sleepless toil of the long night with the sweetness of her song. Whence Basil, in the same place: the song of the psalms is a shield in the terrors of the night, a rest from various labors, a protection from harm, an ornament for the young, a comfort for the old, a most fitting adornment for women, and so on.

div.head: Brotherly Charity
div.p: Beavers teach us brotherly charity. Which, as it is said in the book On the Natures of Things, live in a herd, love their own kind, cut down wood with their teeth, and carry it to their dens in a wonderful way. For they place one of the highest rank on its back, with its feet raised, to serve as a wagon, and lay the cut wood between its legs, and drag it, thus loaded, to their dens, where they unload it and skillfully prepare their dwellings. This, then, teaches us to fulfill that law of charity of which it is said: bear one another's burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ — to the Galatians, chapter 6.

Likewise, stags teach us that the stronger ought to go before the weaker in labors, so that the weaker may lean their heads upon the flanks of the stronger by turns. For, as Solinus says in chapter 27, when crossing the sea, they place the weak ones last, and support the heads of the weary upon their haunches by turns. So too the stronger among us ought to bear the weakness of the weak — to the Romans, chapter 15.

div.head: Carnal Men, Likened to Vultures
div.p: Carnal men are like vultures. For, as Jerome says, flying on high, the vulture spies a carcass below, and for love of the carcass abandons the height of the air and lowers itself to the depths; and when it rises again, it beats its wings against the wind, and rises from the depths into the air more by the aid of the wind than by its own strength. So too carnal men, for the sake of the carcass of carnal delight, descend to the filthy depths, and once they have given themselves to such things, they scarcely draw back from them; and so, for the sake of such delight, they descend from the dignity of the spirit to the filthiness of the flesh. The Psalmist: man, when he was in honor... and so on. Yet if such a man, after his fall, is to rise again, it is necessary that, at the coming — that is, the breath — of the Holy Spirit, he strike the wing of the mind and the wing of works through penance, and so rise on high more by the grace of the Holy Spirit than by his own strength. Likewise, the more the care of the flesh grows in a man, the more it holds back the soul from good, just as we see that the vulture, on account of the abundance of its flesh, flies slowly; so too the body, being corruptible, weighs down and depresses the soul.

div.head: Our Flesh
div.p: Our flesh is like the cow, which, once fattened, casts off the yoke, and, when less well fed, submits to it more readily; but lying and growing sluggish in its own dung, it grows fat. So too our flesh, fattened by the indulgence of gluttony and by the dung of luxury and idleness, kicks back and always refuses to bear the yoke. Deuteronomy 32: my beloved grew fat, and kicked.

Our flesh must be tamed like a young heifer. For a heifer is a young cow, already fit for the yoke. Which, as Isidore says, because it is a wanton creature, is pressed with a stronger yoke and goaded with the prod, that it may rightly follow the ox; so too the wanton flesh ought to be pressed with the strong yoke of penance, and troubled with the goad of penal works.

Likewise, it is likened to the sirens, which are monsters having, from the navel upward, the form of a virgin, but the rest the form of a fish. For, as the Physiologus says, by the sweetness of their song they lull a man to sleep, and when they see him asleep, they attack him unaware and tear his flesh apart. The siren is the desire of the flesh, whose song's sweetness is the delight of the flesh, or the suggestion of delight, to which a man falls asleep when, through negligence, he does not resist; by which, through sin, the soul is laid low and devoured by the habit of sinning. Isaiah 14: sirens in the shrines of pleasure, and so on.

Likewise, it is likened to the scorpion, whose venom, as Pliny says, harms grievously for three days and at last kills by a slow death, unless help comes quickly; so too the desire of the flesh harms over three days — first by pleasurable thought, second by the giving of consent, third by the completion of the act — and so it destroys through the sin of lust, because it leads to eternal death, unless the remedy of penance comes quickly.

Likewise, the vices of the flesh are removed by the persistence of good work, after the example of the roe. Whose flesh, as it is said, is purged of excess by the persistence of motion and by speed, and the heaviness of taste and smell is removed from its flesh. So too, through the running of good work and the constant motion of labor, our flesh is freed from the passions of carnal vice, whose nourishment is idleness. Ecclesiasticus 32: idleness has taught much wickedness.

Likewise, a man better escapes the temptation of the flesh by fleeing than by resisting, just as the roe defends itself from dogs not by claw or tooth, but by fleeing through speed alone. First Corinthians 6: flee fornication.

div.head: Caution against the Assaults of Demons
div.p: Doves teach us caution against the assaults of demons, for, according to the Philosopher in Book VIII on hawks... [the text breaks off incomplete at this point in the source manuscript].

div.head: The Cloistered Life
div.p: ...there are three kinds of fowlers: some do not catch doves except on the ground, others only in the trees, others only flying in the air; and the doves, recognizing all of this, when they see one of these hunters, move to the place where that kind does not strike; so too, and so on.

Bees teach the cloistered life. Of which Pliny says, in Book 11, that they know nothing except what is common to all. But Ambrose, in the Hexameron, teaches: bees seem to tend a kind of commonwealth; alone among all kinds of living creatures they have offspring common to all, dwell in one home, share a common labor, common food, common produce, and common flight. So too the cloistered, and so on.

div.head: Escaping Blindness of Mind
div.p: The lizard teaches us to escape blindness of mind. Which, as Jorach says, when it grows old, its eyes grow dim and it becomes blind; then it turns toward the sun, facing its rays, and directs its eyes at a certain time in the morning, until its sight returns and it sees perfectly, as before. So too the sinner, blinded by sins, ought to direct the eyes of his mind — that is, his understanding, through prayer, and his affection, through devotion — toward the rays of Christ the sun, and so his eyes will be opened by the light of heavenly grace. Isaiah 35: the eyes of the blind shall be opened...

div.head: Spiritual Food
div.p: The example of the camel teaches how spiritual food ought to be received. For, as the book On the Natures of Things says, it has four stomachs: the first receives the raw food, the second somewhat digested, the third more digested, the fourth completely digested. So too the food of spiritual teaching requires four receptacles: it must first be received in the ear, and there attentively heard; second, in the heart, that it may be understood and kept in memory; third, in the hand — that is, fulfilled in deed; fourth, in the mouth, that it may be wisely taught — and this is the complete digestion of the word. Matthew 5: whoever does and teaches these commandments...

div.head: Thoughts
div.p: Thoughts, like birds flying near the ground, are caught more quickly; so too men who think earthly thoughts, and busy themselves with them, are caught by the devil. Bees settle upon flowers and draw honey from them; so too the just, thinking on earthly things, draw sweetness from them. But flies frequent clean places and stain them; so too sinners sometimes take unclean thoughts even from clean things.

div.head: Confessing and Purging Sins
div.p: Dogs teach us to confess and purge our sins. For, as Pliny says in Book 25, this animal seems to have first shown vomiting to man. For dogs find a root which causes disgust, and, having eaten it, vomit when they are too full. So too a sinner, eating the root of penance — that is, contrition — vomits his sins through confession. Ecclesiasticus 21: vomit it out, and it will refresh you.
Likewise, a green frog thrown into a dog's mouth makes it fall silent, just as shame silences a sinner from confessing his sin. Isaiah 56: dumb dogs, unable to bark.

div.head: Confidence, Like the Lion's Strength
div.p: The lion's confidence is like its strength. Whose whole strength, as Isidore says, is in its chest, its firmness in its head. So too the whole firmness and strength of the saints is in the chest — that is, in the heart — and in the head, that is, in the mind. Proverbs 28: the just, like a confident lion, shall be without dread.

div.head: Compunction
div.p: Compunction casts out the arrows of sin. For Aristotle says that when the roe is wounded, it seeks out cumin and eats it, by which it casts the arrows from its body; so too the wounded sinner eats cumin when, through humility, he suppresses the swelling of pride. For cumin-seed checks the swelling of the belly.

div.head: The Contemplative Life
div.p: The contemplative life and abstinence are signified in those fish that were permitted to the Jews under the Law. For it is said in Leviticus 11: whatever has fins and scales, whether in the sea or in the rivers, you shall eat — literally, the eel and similar creatures, lacking fins and scales, were forbidden to the Jews because of their excess of moisture; but morally, by the fins is understood the contemplative life, and by the scales the austere life, both of which are necessary for spiritual cleanliness.

Likewise, the contemplative are likened to birds that sing sweetly, such as the nightingale and the blackbird, which love the woods, nest in trees and thickets, and sing sweetly while warming their eggs. So too the contemplative seek solitary places, and set the nest of the mind — that is, of quiet — in the branches of the tree and the thicket, that is, in the examples, deeds, and footsteps of the humble and devout, and there sweetly praise God, whether with the voice, or in the mind, or both.

Likewise, they are likened to the kingfisher. Of which Ambrose says, in the Hexameron: the kingfisher is a sea-bird which, in the very midst of winter, when the sea rises highest and is beaten by the waves, broods her eggs on the seashore and hatches them in seven days, which she then nurses for another seven days; whence sailors observe these fourteen days as a presumed calm, and call them the 'halcyon days.' If, then, so small a bird has such power that, by the mere sight of her brooding, she makes the raging sea calm, how much more should a rational creature, since it can still all the tempestuous stirrings of the heart. For this bird, though she sees the stormy sea, does not fear to lay her eggs on the shore, nor does she depart before the proper rearing of her young; so too, and so on.

Likewise, the contemplative rest in the highest places, just as the eagle sets its nest in steep heights, as Aristotle says in Book VIII, for the eagle does not nest in the plains, but in cliffs and in trees.

Likewise, stags dwell in the mountains, according to that verse of the Psalms: 'The high mountains are for the stags,' and so on. As a sign of this, the Lord, wishing to pray, went up into a mountain, where he was also transfigured before them, that the contemplative too might rest, not in the lowest places, but in the highest, through love...

div.head: Continence
div.p: Vultures teach us virginal continence. Which, according to Ambrose in Book V of the Hexameron, are said to conceive and bring forth without mating.

Likewise the bees, for, as the same author says in the same place, bees mate with no union, are not dissolved by desire, nor shaken by the pains of childbirth, but, preserving the virginal integrity of their bodies, suddenly send forth a great swarm of offspring. Virgil, in the fourth book of the Georgics: marvel that they are so pleased with this custom, that they indulge in no mating, nor grow slack in Venus, nor bring forth their young in labor.
Wood-pigeons teach the continence of widowhood. Which, as Aristotle says, naturally love one another, and keep this continence too: that if one loses its mate, it does not mate again.
The turtledove does the same. Which, as Ambrose says, is a chaste bird, which, if widowed by the loss of its own mate, refuses to renew its union, and does not know how to break faith with the first.

The lion teaches conjugal continence. For, as Pliny says, by scent it perceives the mating of the leopard with an adulterous mate, and rises with all its force to punish it; for this fault the lioness is washed in a river and long shunned.
Likewise, the continence of chastity brings the prolonging of life. Whence the vulture, which mates with no union, lives a hundred years, as Isidore says.

div.head: Conversion
div.p: Conversion is not to be delayed, just as a bird, which, seeing the bow drawn and the arrow ready, does not delay its flight. So the Psalmist: unless you are converted, and so on — up to: he has bent his bow, and so on. Ecclesiasticus 5: do not delay to be converted, and so on.

div.head: Contrition
div.p: Contrition. Just as the living fly is food for the spider, but crushed and placed upon the spider's bite, it draws out the venomous poison and eases the pain; so too sin, living in a man, feeds the devil, but when it is put to death through penance and contrition, it repels the temptations of demons.

div.head: The Heart
div.p: The devil attacks the heart in man first, just as the hawk attacks its prey. For the hawk seeks the heart first, since, being a hot-blooded bird, it requires rich nourishment, which is the heart. Likewise it wishes to turn the whole prey to its own use, and so it begins with the heart, which is the root and fountain of life; so too the devil hopes to have everything, once he has the heart. Yet this may be taken in a good sense too: that God, like a noble bird, seeks the heart first, according to that verse: 'Give me your heart.'

Likewise, the heart must be cleansed, that it may be a fitting dwelling for God. For Aristotle says in Book IV that a fish approaches a new, clean vessel more readily than an old one; indeed, unless it is new, it rarely approaches the old one at all. So too God does not approach the vessel of the heart unless it is new and clean... The Psalmist: create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me, and so on.

div.head: The Curious
div.p: The curious are like stags. For the stag, as Pliny says in Book VIII, is struck with wonder at everything, and so more easily offers itself to those who would shoot it. So too curious minds, while they marvel at and linger over novelties, are more easily struck by the devil with the dart of error or of sin.

div.head: The Cruel
div.p: The cruel, such as tyrants or plunderers, often die of hunger, even as beggars, after the example of the eagle, of which Aristotle says in Book VIII that as eagles grow old, their beak grows longer, and, being always turned upward, it hinders them, so that in the end they die more of hunger. The fable says that this happens to it because it once, when it was strange to it, marveled at a man.
Likewise, they are like dogs, which attack the afflicted. The Psalmist: they have added to the pain of my wounds.

div.head: The Cross of Christ
div.p: The Cross of Christ laid the devil low. An example of this we have in the wild ox, which hates and pursues everything red; therefore the hunter clothes himself in red, and the ox pursues him, and when it sees him drawing near, he hides himself behind a tree, and then the ox, wishing to kill him, drives its horns so forcefully into the tree that it becomes stuck there, and so is captured. The devil bears the likeness of this ox, which pursues everything red, thirsting without ceasing for the blood of the saints; so too Christ, the hunter, clothed himself in red in his Passion, and hid himself behind the tree of the cross, into which the devil, wishing to drive his horns, struck instead, and so destroyed himself.

div.head: The Slanderer
div.p: The slanderer is likened to the serpent called the dipsas. Which, as Isidore says, is said to be of such smallness that, when trodden upon, it is not seen. Its venom kills before it is felt, and the face of the dying man, overtaken by death, shows no sign of sorrow. Such is the secret slanderer. Ecclesiasticus 4: he who slanders in secret is no different from one who is bitten by a serpent in silence.

Likewise, the serpent moves in a crooked path. Whence, according to Isidore, it is called 'anguis,' as if 'angular,' because it never moves in a straight line; such is the deceitful slanderer, who begins with praise, so as not to seem to speak from hatred, but then turns it round to abuse.

Third, because the serpent eats earth. For there are certain serpents, as Pliny says, that hide in caves, lick the dust, and flee the moisture of the earth; so too the slanderer, who lies in wait for others, hides himself, and eats only what he sees as earthly, base, and defective, biting and slandering it. Isaiah 65: the dust of the earth shall be the serpent's bread. But if he sees anything good, he suppresses it.

Likewise, Isidore says in the book of Etymologies: the lion does not eat man, except in the greatest necessity of hunger. Slanderers do the opposite: once they are sated, they begin to tear men apart.
Likewise, according to the Philosopher, animals that devour raw flesh have foul-smelling mouths; so too do slanderers. The Psalmist: their throat is an open sepulcher, and so on.

div.head: The Delight of Sin
div.p: The delight of sin kills the mind, just as a drink kills a mouse. For Aristotle says in a certain book that a mouse, if it drinks water, will die; delight, likewise, is drunk in when consent is given to it.

Likewise, delight is a cause of the soul's death, just as the sweetness of honey is a cause of the bear's death. For, as the book On the Natures of Things says, bears climb trees for the sake of honey; hunters, having noted this, hang a mallet there, and when the bear, eager for honey, finds this mallet in its way and throws it off, it is struck all the more violently by it as it swings back, and is killed. Likewise, while a man seeks sweetness, the mallet of the divine word hinders and delays him; and the more forcefully and the longer he casts it away from himself, the more he rushes into sin and, at last, into destruction.

div.head: The Devil
div.p: The devil is likened to the owl. For, as Aristotle says in Book VIII, the other birds fly around the owl and pluck out its feathers, and many kinds of birds hate it.

Likewise, as the book On the Natures of Things says, it flees the light, dwells in churches, drinks the oil from the lamps, and fouls them with its droppings. So too the devil is hated by the saints and plucked bare — that is, stripped of his malice — and flees the light of grace. Likewise he strives to empty the oil of charity and grace from the lamps of the saints, and, where he can, tries to stain the good hearts of sinners with filth.

Likewise, he is likened to the night-raven, of which Ambrose says in the Hexameron: 'the night-raven does not feel the horror of nightly darkness,' and the darker the night is, the more unhindered its flight; but by day it cannot see, because its sight is dulled by the brightness. So too the devil flees the light of grace, because he is dulled by its brightness, and loves the darkness of sin; and the thicker the darkness among sinners, the more unhindered he makes his flights.

Likewise, he is likened to the dragon. For Isidore says: the dragon has its power in its tail, not in its teeth, and harms more by a blow than by a bite; whatever it binds, it kills. So too the whole power of the devil is in his 'tail,' in deception, and whatever he binds, he finally kills in the soul.
Likewise, he is likened to that serpent which, as Pliny says in Book XII, dares not touch a naked man. So too the devil does not attack the poor in spirit.
Likewise, he is likened to the snake called coluber, which, as Isidore says, is so named as if 'dweller in shadows.'

Likewise, he is likened to the wolf. First, by reason of fraud and deception. For it is said in the book On the Natures of Things that it sometimes gathers willow-leaves in its mouth and hides beneath them, so as secretly to seize the goats that come for the leaves. A certain kind of wolf also imitates human voices, and so deceives shepherds; it also deceives dogs by whining like a dog. So too the devil sometimes transforms himself into an angel of light, in order to deceive. Aristotle also says that in India there is a kind of wolf that has the face of a man and the tail of a scorpion; so too the devil at first seems to persuade with reasonable things, but in the end pours in his venom. The devil also hides himself beneath green leaves, when he deceives us under the appearance of good things.
Second, by reason of ferocity. For, as Pliny says in Book VIII, the wolf is strong and bold and fierce, not fearful; so too the devil.

Likewise the wolf, as Ambrose says in the Hexameron, if it sees a man first, steals his voice, and, as a victor, looks down on him for the loss of his voice. Pliny, in Book VIII, and Solinus, in chapter 2, say these are found in Italy; but if the man sees the wolf first, the wolf loses its boldness and drops its tail. So too the devil, like the wolf, gets ahead of a man when he sees him not resisting at the outset; but if the man instead gets ahead of the devil, arming himself to repel the beginning of temptation, then the devil loses his boldness and lowers the tail of his deception, because he ceases to tempt.

Likewise, he is likened to the fox, for, according to the Philosopher in Book I, it is a cunning and malicious animal; whence, according to Isidore, it is called 'vulpes' as if 'volipes' [twisting-foot], because it never runs in a straight path, but in crooked windings — a deceitful animal, tricking by ambush, sometimes feigning itself dead, so that it may catch birds descending to it as to a carcass. All these things can be applied to the devil.

div.head: Loving All Men, but Hating Sin
div.p: We ought to love all men, but hate sin, after the example of the panther, of which Isidore says that it is a friend to all animals except the dragon. So too a man ought to be a friend to every man, but an enemy to the dragon — that is, to sin. Whence Augustine, in the book of Sentences of Prosper: men are to be loved in such a way that their errors are not loved; it is one thing to love what they are, and another to hate what they do.

div.head: Preachers, Likened to Cocks
div.p: Preachers are likened to cocks. First, on account of their marking of the times. For, as Pliny says in Book X, cocks, the night-watchmen, which nature made to rouse men to their work, know the stars, and announce the third hour of the day by their crowing and clapping. And Ambrose, in the Hexameron: the cock rouses the sleeper, relieves the anxious, comforts the traveler; at its crowing the thief abandons his ambush; at its call the morning star itself is roused and lights up the sky; the fearful sailor lays aside his gloom, and every storm risen from the winds and gusts of evening grows gentle. All these things can be applied, one by one, to the preacher.

Likewise, as Gregory says in the Moralia, when the cock prepares to crow, it first shakes itself with its wings, and, striking itself, makes itself more watchful; so too holy preachers first exercise themselves in good works, which they then preach to others.

Third, as Gregory says, in the deeper hours of the night they send forth stronger voices and songs, but gentler ones near dawn; so too the preacher, when he speaks to sinners more deeply sunk in sin, ought to speak more forcefully, whether of divine judgment or of eternal punishment; but as the light of grace begins to dawn, he ought to speak more gently — that is, of divine mercies, of eternal rewards, and the like.

div.head: The Deceitful
div.p: The deceitful man is likened to the weasel-like creature called the migale, an animal shaped like a weasel, deceitful, but feigning gentleness; when it sees something approach, it soon leaps upon it and pours in its venom. So too many deceitful men feign gentleness and friendship, but, once the opportunity arises, do harm. Ecclesiasticus 11: many are the snares of the deceitful.
Likewise, he is likened to the fox, of which above, in the chapter on the Devil.

div.head: The House of the Mind
div.p: A man ought carefully to build the house of his mind, after the example of the beaver. Which, as the book On the Natures of Things says, builds its house from wood, which it cuts with its teeth, over the water, making various chambers in it, so that, as the water rises or falls, it may go up or down. So too a man ought to build his house upon the waters of compunction or of wisdom, so that, as the water of wisdom rises, he may be raised to the contemplation of heavenly things, or, as the water of compunction or tribulation rises, the soul may rise still further to the perfection of purity and virtue; but the more it decreases, the lower it falls.

div.head: Hard Hearts
div.p: Hard hearts are not cleansed by scourges. They are like the crocodile, whose hide is so hard that, though it receives the blow of heavy stones upon its back, it takes no notice. Such was Pharaoh, whose heart was hardened, so that through many plagues he would not let the people go; so too the hardened sinner, even scourged, does not let go of his sin. Bernard, in Book V of the Consideration: a hard heart — one that is not torn by compunction, nor softened by mercy, nor moved by entreaties — does not yield to threats or harsh scourges; ungrateful for kindnesses, faithless in counsel, savage in judgment, shameless in disgrace, fearless of dangers, inhuman toward human things, rash toward divine things, forgetting the past, neglecting the present, not providing for the future — there is in it altogether no foresight of future dangers, except perhaps to take revenge.

div.head: The Elect, Likened to Sheep
div.p: The elect are likened to sheep. First, on account of innocence. For, as Isidore says, the sheep is a gentle flock-animal, unarmed in body and covered only in wool. And so we see that nature gave it no weapons: no horns to strike with, no claws to tear with, no teeth to bite with, but only to graze; so too the elect harm no one. To the Romans 14: what have these sheep done.

Second, on account of the abundance of their milk, fleece, and offspring. There are four things that make them abundant in offspring: wind, drink, pasture, and motion — for, as Aristotle says, if sheep conceive facing the north wind, they bear males; if facing the south, females. So too the truly elect do more manly deeds in time of adversity than in time of prosperity.

Second is drink, whence Aristotle says, in the same place, that sheep drinking salt water are more inclined to mate, and, it follows, likewise to bear young; so too the elect, drinking the water of wisdom, become more ready and more fruitful in good works.
Third is pasture, especially at the end of the day, which, as the book On the Natures of Things says, helps them toward generation.

Third, by reason of abstinence, for the book On the Natures of Things says: sheep led to pasture in dry places live long, but those pastured in marshy places become diseased, and cannot live long. Therefore Palladius teaches, in Book XII: in the summer months let them graze at the break of day, when the mingling of dew recommends the sweetness of the tender grass, but while grazing the head must always be turned away from the sun. So too the elect are preserved by the dryness of abstinence, and are fed with the mingling of the dew of grace, if they turn the head — that is, the mind — away from the sun of present prosperity, for the sake of fellowship and social life. For, as Pliny says in Book XXX, thunder brings on miscarriage in solitary sheep, and the remedy for them is to gather together, that they may be helped by the flock; so too solitary and unsocial men frequently miscarry the good that they have conceived.

div.head: Giving Alms
div.p: The eagle teaches us to give alms. Which, as Pliny says, is of such generosity that it does not eat the prey it has caught alone, unless it is exceedingly hungry, but divides the food among the birds that follow it. And so, Luke 11: give as alms what remains over.

div.head: The Evangelists, the Horses of Christ
div.p: The evangelists are the horses of Christ. For, as Isidore says, they are called 'equi' because they are matched together in a team; this team is the holy Church, in which are the four Gospels, and so on.

Likewise, they are called the 'caballi' of Christ. 'Caballus' is so named from the hollow of the foot, because its pressed hoof hollows out the earth, as Isidore says; this hollowing of the earth is the emptying-out of earthly love.

Likewise, they were the resounding-footed steeds of Christ. Which, according to Isidore, are so called because they resound with their feet: for they resounded not only with the mouth, in preaching, but with the footsteps of their works, in teaching.

div.head: Exaltation
div.p: As Pliny says in Book V, the crow, when the hard shell of a nut resists its beak, carries it up on high and repeatedly drops it upon a stone, until, shattered, it breaks. So too the devil, unable to break a man, lifts him up to high rank, so as to cast him down into sin. Job 30: you have lifted me up, and, setting me as it were upon the wind, have violently dashed me down.

div.head: Excommunication
div.p: Excommunication is likened to the bite of a rabid dog, since every animal bitten by a rabid dog becomes rabid itself; so too all who associate with an excommunicated person, in cases not permitted, themselves become excommunicated, and therefore such persons are to be avoided as one avoids a rabid dog.

div.head: The Examples of the Saints
div.p: The examples of the saints who went before us teach us to despise earthly things. For Pliny says that the bones of cocks and hens are poison to gold; so too the bones and examples of the saints teach the contempt of gold and of earthly things.

div.head: The Fervor of the Spirit
div.p: The fervor of the spirit consumes the wantonness of the flesh, just as the fervor of natural heat consumes the fatness of the body — which is seen in the camel, of which Constantine says that it is by nature an exceedingly hot animal, and therefore lean, because its heat consumes its fat and the richness of its blood; so too the fervor of divine love consumes the desires of the flesh. James 1: the sun rose with its burning heat, and withered the grass. Isaiah 40: all flesh is grass, and so on.

div.head: The False Penitent
div.p: The false penitent is likened to the toad called the rubeta, which, as the book On the Natures of Things says, sheds and takes on again its old skin, but never sheds its venom. So too the false penitent seems to change his outward skin, but always keeps the venom — that is, sin — within. Pliny, in Book VIII, says: the rubeta, stocked with many remedies, is said to shed and take up its venoms daily through its diet, whence they are always kept in reserve within it. So too, and so on.

div.head: Children's Duty toward Their Parents
div.p: Storks teach children to be devoted to their parents. For, as Aristotle says in Book VIII, it is commonly said of storks that the chicks feed their aging parents. Basil says the same.
Likewise, crows feed their young in youth, but the young, in turn, feed their parents in old age, and, when they grow weak, carry them upon their shoulders.

Likewise, Ambrose says that crows, when their parents are stripped of feathers in old age, feed the younger ones with gathered food, support them with the prop of their own wings, and train them to fly, so as to bring their disused limbs back to their former use.

Likewise, the Physiologus says: the young of the hoopoe, when they see that their parents have grown so old that they can neither fly nor see, pluck out their parents' oldest feathers, anoint their eyes, and warm them beneath their wings, until their feathers grow back and their eyes are given light again; and thus they repay their parents in kind.

div.head: Deceit
div.p: The deceit of demons or of heretics is likened to the partridge. Of which Ambrose says, in the Hexameron: the partridge is a cunning bird, which breaks open the eggs of another partridge and broods them with her own body, but gains no advantage from her fraud, for when she has hatched the chicks, they leave her and follow their true mother, who laid the eggs. Jeremiah 1: the partridge has brooded eggs she did not lay. So too the devil or the heretic, as it were, seizes another's eggs, when he cunningly deceives and draws to himself the children of Holy Church; but he often labors in vain, for such children, on returning, follow their true mother, the Church.

Likewise, he is likened to the crab, which, as Ambrose says, feeds on oysters; but since it cannot force open a closed oyster, it waits until the oyster opens itself to the rays of the sun, and then secretly slips in a stone, so that the oyster cannot close again, and thus eats it, once opened. So too the deceitful man tricks others and feeds on their misfortune.

div.head: The Chatterer
div.p: The chatterer is likened to the jackdaw. Which, as Isidore says, is so named from its chattering, for it is a most talkative kind, and troublesome with its noise. The book On the Natures of Things also says that it flits chattering from one tree to another, and no one can pass by whom it does not chatter against; but when caught young, it learns to speak articulate words, and sometimes, while intent on its chattering and not looking about, a hawk's swoop seizes it unexpectedly. All these things fit the chatterer, and sometimes befall him.

div.head: Grace
div.p: Heavenly grace feeds only the undefiled. For the Gloss, on the verse 'and to the young ravens that call upon him,' says: the chicks of ravens are said to feed on the dew of heaven, and, by the kindness of their youth, are ignorant of ordinary food — that is, the stench of carrion. For this bird, as Isidore says, is born with white feathers, and therefore its parents do not feed it until it grows to resemble them and turns black; so then, as long as they are white, they feed on the dew of heaven — so too innocent and clean men feed on the grace of God.

Likewise, it is likened to the bird called the caladrius. For, as the Physiologus says, if a sick man is to die, it does not look at him; but if he can recover, it looks at him, and, drawing all his sicknesses to itself, the bird itself becomes sick and often dies for him. So too the grace of the Holy Spirit does not look upon the sinner who is hopeless through infernal impenitence, but looks upon the one who is curable, and, drawing all his sicknesses to itself, makes him whole.

Likewise, grace is likened to the heart, or to the root-organ in an animal that stands in the place of the heart; for just as the formation and shaping of an animal begins from the heart, so too creation, spiritual formation, and the shaping of the virtues begins from grace, which is the fountain and origin of the whole spiritual life.

Likewise, grace does not admit a man to its consolation as long as he carries sin in his conscience, just as the foal of a horse, which is born with a black caul on its forehead, is not admitted to its mother's udder until this is cut away; so too, unless sin is cut away through penance, the consolation of grace is not received.

div.head: Gratitude for Kindness
div.p: The panther teaches us to be grateful for kindnesses. Which, as Pliny relates, attached itself to a man who had freed her cubs from a pit into which they had fallen, and, fawning as if to show gratitude, led him safely out of the wilderness. To the Colossians 3: be grateful.

Likewise, the sparrowhawk, of which Albert says, in Book XXIII of the Animals, that when it catches a bird in winter, it holds it in its feet for the sake of warmth, on account of the harsh cold. Whence, just as it lets it go alive, so too, and so on.

div.head: The Gluttonous
div.p: The gluttonous are likened to the kite. Which, as Pliny says, is a most rapacious bird, and always hungry, which, out of gluttony, feeds on filthy things, and wanders and roams about widely for the sake of little food; so too the gluttonous, and so on.

Likewise, they are like the crocodile, which gladly feeds on plants, among which a small serpent, its enemy, hides itself, so that, while it grazes on the plants, it swallows the serpent, which then kills it, and comes out of its belly unharmed. So too the glutton, while he often eats savory morsels, frequently swallows the poison of pleasure, which kills his mind.

div.head: Abundance
div.p: Abundance of earthly prosperity does not allow one to feel the wounds of the mind. Just as the whale is of such fatness that it does not feel a wound unless the whole layer of fat is pierced through to the flesh — for then, not feeling the bitterness of the water, it makes for the shore, or dies quickly — so too those who abound in wealth do not feel their griefs, unless they are wounded in their innermost parts, when something they greatly loved is taken from them; and then, struck by compunction for their sins, they seek the shore of penance, but often die quickly through despair.

div.head: Heretics
div.p: Heretics are likened to the whale. Of which Jorach says, in his book On the Animals, that when it grows old, dust gathers and thickens upon its back so much that it looks like an island, so that sailors, approaching it carelessly, can scarcely escape without danger: for it throws up such a quantity of water over the ship from its mouth that it sometimes capsizes it. So too heretics sometimes present a semblance of solidity in holiness, and those who draw near them are overwhelmed by the waters of false wisdom.

div.head: Modesty and Chastity in Marriage
div.p: Elephants teach us modesty and chastity in the continence of marriage. Which, as Pliny says, out of modesty, never mate except in hiding; and, as Aristotle says in Book V, once the female has conceived, she is not touched at all by the male, and she carries her young for two years. So too modesty ought to be kept in marriage, as to place and time.

div.head: Humility
div.p: Humility makes the mind keen-sighted for contemplation. Isidore, in the book of Etymologies: the fish called the aphya is so small that it cannot be caught with a hook — such is the smallness of humility. For, as Avicenna says, the eagle's eye is small, and yet most keen-sighted for looking at the light of the sun; but the eye of the night-raven is large, and yet cannot gaze upon the light of the sun. The small eye is the humble mind, which sees the true sun; the large eye is the proud mind, which, the prouder it is, the more darkened it is toward seeing divine things.

Likewise, it contributes to spiritual fruitfulness, for, according to Pliny in Book X, the larger animals are, the less fruitful they are. To the Ephesians: elephants, camels, and horses bear one young; the smallest bird bears a dozen. So too the humble man brings forth many offspring of good works.

div.head: Fleeing Incest
div.p: The horse teaches us to flee incest. For, as Aristotle says in Book VIII, a man once covered the head of a mare, with which her own son then mated with his head covered; but once his head was uncovered and he recognized his mother, he fled and threw himself off a cliff. Likewise the camel: with the mother's head covered, its offspring mounted her; but afterward, recognizing whom it had mated with, it soon after bit and killed the keeper who had been the cause of it. How much more, then, ought a man to abhor such things and their like. Deuteronomy 27: cursed is he who lies with his father's wife.

div.head: The Inconstant
div.p: The inconstant man is like the hyena. Of which Pliny says, in a certain book, that it has the nature of both male and female, becoming male in alternate years and female in others, and that the common people believe it can bear young without a male, though Aristotle denies this. So too the inconstant man is sometimes found male — that is, robust in intention — but afterward found female in deed; or manly at the outset, but womanish and weak as things go on.

div.head: Avoiding Marital Incontinence
div.p: Stags teach us to avoid marital incontinence. Of which Pliny says, in Book VIII, that from the time of conception the females are kept apart from the males until they are purified from giving birth; so too, and so on.

div.head: Illness of the Body
div.p: Sickness of the body is sometimes a medicine for the mind, as Solinus says in a certain chapter, that the lion suffers from a quartan fever, which seems to happen by God's providence, so that its wrathfulness may be tempered. Seneca: I give thanks for my sickness, which compels me not to be able to do what I ought not wish to do.

Likewise, elephants, when they are sick, are said to gather certain healing herbs, which, before they eat them, they lift up toward heaven, their heads raised, as if, by a kind of religious observance, asking help from God. So too a man, when he suffers something, ought to seek help from God...

div.head: Ingratitude
div.p: Ingratitude excludes children from their father's inheritance. Whence, as the book On the Natures of Things says, the pelican — the mother bird — over her young, killed by a serpent, strikes her own breast and pours out her own blood to bring them back to life; and once it is poured out, she becomes so weak that she cannot leave the nest, so her chicks are forced to go out both to feed her and to feed themselves. Of these chicks, she greatly loves those who, with filial devotion, feed her once she regains her strength; but the others, who feed themselves and neglect their mother, she casts out and despises. So too grateful children are to be loved and nourished by their parents, but the ungrateful cast out. This pelican also represents Christ to us, according to the verse 'I have become like the pelican of the wilderness,' who loves the grateful children brought to life by his blood, but rightly excludes the ungrateful from the eternal inheritance.

div.head: Persecutors of the Innocent
div.p: The persecutors of the innocent are crueler than sea-beasts, for Jorach says, in his book On the Animals, that dolphins can tell, by scent, if a man drowned at sea has eaten dolphin-flesh; and if he has eaten it, they eat him in turn, but if he has not, they guard him from the bites of other fish and bring him to the shore. But alas! Some men are crueler still, for Aesop says: the harmful man harms the harmless, and finds a cause for doing harm.

div.head: Punishing Disobedience
div.p: Bees teach that disobedience must be punished. Which, as Ambrose says, when they disobey their king, exact vengeance upon themselves, and kill themselves with the blade of their own sting.

div.head: The Impatient
div.p: The impatient man is likened to the bear, which, being a wrathful and impatient animal, wishes to avenge itself on each one separately; so that when it attacks someone, if another attacks it, it at once lets the first go and attacks the other; but when it is captured, it is blinded by the sight of a glowing basin, and bound with a chain. So too the impatient man, wishing to avenge himself on each and every one, is at last blinded, by raging anger, in the judgment of reason, and therefore must be bound with chains and tamed with blows.

div.head: Those Who Do Not Persevere
div.p: Those who do not persevere are like the leopard. Which, as the Physiologus says, catches its prey not by chasing it, but by leaping; and if it does not catch it in the third or fourth leap, it gives up out of indignation and, as it were, defeated, draws back. So too some, not obtaining at once what they want, give up the work they began, not considering that persistent labor conquers all things. Luke 11: if he persists in knocking, and so on.

div.head: The Unstable and Inconstant
div.p: The unstable and inconstant man is likened to the chameleon. Which, as Solinus says, has a color that varies and changes in a moment, so that it takes on the color of whatever thing it touches. For no animal is found, as Isidore says, that so readily takes on the changing colors of opposites. So too the unstable mind, and so on.

div.head: Envy
div.p: The envious man is likened to the peacock. For, as Jerome says against Jovinian, peacock dung is said to relieve the burning of gout. And so Pliny says, in Book 21, that the envious, out of ill-will toward the benefit of men, swallow back their own dung.

Likewise, he is likened to stags, which hide their shed antlers, begrudging their usefulness to men, as Aristotle says in a certain book. So too the envious grieve if anyone derives benefit from them.
Likewise, they are like the sirens, which rejoice in a storm and grieve in fair weather. So too the envious grieve at the prosperity of others and rejoice at their misfortunes.

Likewise, he is likened to the salamander. Which, as Pliny says in Book X, is of such coldness that it extinguishes fire no less than ice does. So too the envious man extinguishes the fire of charity.

Likewise, they are likened to the lynx. Of which Isidore says that its urine turns into the stone called ligurium, which the lynx, once it has passed it, covers with sand out of a certain envy of nature, lest such an excretion pass into human use; so too, and so on.

Likewise, he is likened to the dragon. Of which Pliny says that it has its venom in its tongue and its gall, and that, by the force of its venom, its tongue is always raised, and by the heat of its breath the air is set aflame, so that it sometimes seems to be on fire; it has its whole power in its tail, for whatever its tail binds, it kills; it has the keenest sight, and sees its prey from far off. Likewise the envious man has the venom of hatred in his gall — that is, inwardly, in his mind — and in his tongue — that is, in slander — and his tongue is raised to do evil, to speak proudly, and to inflame hatred; he has his whole power in his tail, for he strikes from behind through hidden slander, and kills through defamation; he rarely sleeps — that is, he rarely rests from doing harm and scheming — and he has the keenest sight against his neighbor's faults, so that he sees from afar what he might seize upon against him.

Likewise, he is likened to the butterfly, because, thinking to harm another, he harms himself, just as the butterfly, wishing to extinguish a light, rushes into the flame and burns itself. The Psalmist: let his sorrow be turned upon his own head, and so on.

div.head: The Hypocrite
div.p: The hypocrite is likened to the ostrich, which has feathers, and yet does not fly. So too the hypocrite makes a show of the spiritual life, but does not match it in his works.
Likewise, he is likened to the swan, which has outwardly the whitest feather, but inwardly black flesh; so too the hypocrite outwardly displays the whiteness of holiness, but inwardly, and so on.

Likewise, he is likened to the panther. Of which Solinus says, in chapter 23, that the other animals are drawn by the variety of its color and by its scent, but are terrified by the grimness of its face; therefore it hides that part, and lets the rest of its body be seen, so that it may thus lay waste the stupefied herds by their gaze. So too the hypocrite outwardly displays the beauty of a good life and shows the fragrance of a good reputation, but hides the head of his malice — his corrupt intention.

Likewise, he is likened to the ape. Which, according to Aristotle in the second book of the Animals, is like a man in its outward form, but in its inward parts, where it differs most from man, is like the other animals. So too the hypocrite, and so on.

div.head: Wrath
div.p: Wrath is likened to the bee. Which, as Aristotle says in Book VIII, dies when it stings, because it cannot fix its sting without losing its innards; so too a man, when he stings another in anger, loses the innards of gentleness, and so dies spiritually.

Likewise, the wrathful man is likened to the wild boar. Which, according to Avicenna, is a fierce animal, of such ferocity that it counts death as nothing, and fearlessly rushes upon the hunter's spear. So too Job 5: wrath kills the foolish man.

Likewise, he is likened to a rabid dog. Which, as Constantine says in the Viaticum, other dogs flee, and it wanders alone; it staggers as if drunk, runs with its mouth open, tongue hanging, saliva flowing, its eyes red, and though its eyes are open, it collides with every object as if it were blind, resists everything in its way, and barks at its own shadow. So too the wrathful man wanders alone, unable to bear company. Whence Proverbs 22: do not be a friend to a wrathful man — for he deserves to be avoided by others. He runs with his mouth open, because he does not cease to utter abusive words; his tongue hangs, because he cannot restrain it, for the fool spends his whole breath, from whom the saliva of discretion drips away, and, as if blind, he attacks whatever resists him, whether by hearing or by sight — for he takes offense at every word, custom, or gesture. And so he resists everything he sees or hears, and even alone, by himself, he mutters, and so barks at his own shadow.

Likewise, he is likened to the hedgehog, a spiny animal, which, rolling itself in fallen fruit, takes one piece in its mouth; but if, while carrying them to its den, one falls, it angrily shakes off all the rest and goes back to the tree to load itself again. So too the wrathful man, if something goes against him, destroys all the good he has done.

Likewise, he is like those wrathful animals that bear incomplete offspring, as the dog bears blind pups, and the bear a shapeless mass of flesh, its limbs not yet distinct; so too the wrathful man's works are blind, not preceded by the counsel of reason.
Likewise, his works are confused and disordered, unless they are afterward repaired and shaped by the gentleness of wisdom.

div.head: Judging by the Worth of the Mind, Not the Body
div.p: One ought to judge a man not by the appearance of his body, but by the worth of his mind. An example of this is the hawk, which, according to Isidore, is a royal bird armed more by spirit than by claws; whence what nature denies it in bodily size, its strength of spirit and boldness make up for.

div.head: Washing Away Sins with Tears of Penance
div.p: Elephants teach us to wash away our sins with tears of penance, for, according to Pliny, at the new moon they gather in herds and wash themselves in the river, and then return to their places. So too men, at the 'new moon' — that is, in adversity or new change — ought to flock to the waters of teaching or tearful compunction, and there wash themselves.

div.head: Human Laws
div.p: Human laws are like spiders' webs, as Anacharsis says, for in them small and weak creatures — like flies — are caught and entangled, but the great ones pass through and break free. So too the great, who transgress the law, are not punished, but only the small and weak.

div.head: Patience
div.p: The wild ass teaches us patience. For, as the book On the Natures of Things says, though it is impatient with thirst, it nevertheless waits a long time, until it finds the clearest water, and does not readily drink otherwise. So too a man ought patiently to wait until he drinks from the fountain of eternal life.

div.head: Disordered Games
div.p: Disordered games are an omen or cause of a bad end, just as the play of dolphins is an omen of a coming storm.

div.head: The Lustful
div.p: The lustful man is likened to the he-goat. Of which Isidore says that it is a lascivious and wanton animal, always eager for mating, whose eyes, out of lust, look sideways. Hence its name too, for according to Suetonius, 'hirci' are the corners of the eyes. So too the lustful man has a shameless eye, showing forth a shameless mind, for, according to Augustine, a shameless eye is the messenger of a shameless heart. Second, because the he-goat is always foul-smelling; so too the lustful man stinks through his ill repute.

Third, because, as Pliny says, the he-goat is never without fever; for it is of such heat that its warm blood can soften the diamond stone, which neither iron nor fire can master, and so it suffers a continual fever. So too some men are so wanton that they are always in the heat of evil desire.

Likewise, he is likened to the pig, because, according to Isidore, the pig ('porcus') is named as if 'spurcus' [filthy]; for it gorges itself in filth and buries itself in mud. So too the lustful man, who rests in the filth and stench of carnal sins. Jeremiah 48: he shall remain in his own dregs.
Second, because, as Aristotle says in Book VI, the pig, once it loses one eye, soon dies. So too, since the shameless eye is the incitement of lust, once it is lost, lust ceases and dies.
Third, because pigs lie more in the mud on their right side of prosperity than on their left side of adversity. Ecclesiasticus 6: the wickedness of one hour causes the forgetting of great luxury.

Likewise, he is likened to the moth, which, according to Gregory, is born from the garment, and yet in the end gnaws away the very garment from which it arose. So too lust, as it is said in Job 31, devours utterly and roots out everything.

div.head: Monks, Likened to Fish
div.p: Monks are likened to fish. For Ambrose says that there is a great closeness and kinship between fish and water: for they cannot live long outside the water; so too monks outside the cloister. Whence Isaiah 1: fish shall rot without water — that is, monks without the cloister or the cell.

div.head: The Remembrance of Death
div.p: The remembrance of death brings to nothing all the glory of beauty, after the example of the peacock. Which, as the book On the Natures of Things says, when it sees the beauty of its feathers, raises its tail and forms an arc; but when it beholds the ugliness of its feet, it blushes and lowers its tail. The foot, then, by which the body touches the earth, signifies death, through which the body returns to the earth. Whoever, then, glories in some beauty, is humbled if he thinks again of death. Ecclesiasticus 10: why are you proud, earth and ashes? Likewise, the remembrance of death guides the soul, just as birds and fish steer themselves by their tail. So too a man guides his life by his end.

div.head: Loving Cleanness of Mind
div.p: Bees teach us to love cleanness of mind. Which, as Pliny says, allow no filth among their works; when they can, they carry out and gather in one place the waste they produce within, and cast out the worst of it, for they cannot bear any foul smell. So too a man ought to do clean works, without the filth of sin, and cast out what is unclean through penance, and so on.

div.head: Gifts
div.p: Gifts sometimes soften or change the mind of a judge. For sometimes a suckling puppy runs at someone as if wishing to bite him, but if he throws it a scrap of bread, it takes it and falls silent. So too sometimes a superior barks at some subordinate who needs correcting, as if wishing to devour him, but if that man strikes a bargain, giving a mark of gold or silver, he takes it and falls silent. Ecclesiasticus 33: gifts and presents, and so on.

div.head: Avoiding Negligence
div.p: The eagle teaches us to avoid negligence. Which, as Ambrose says, urges its full-grown chicks to fly by hovering over them, and, if they are slow to leave the nest, strikes them with its beak and withholds their food, and so forces them out. So too Christ urges his children to the flight of good works, and sometimes pricks the slothful with the beak of some tribulation, and so on. Deuteronomy: as an eagle urges its young to fly, hovering over them.

Likewise, Basil says, in the Hexameron, that hawks cast their young from the nest to make them fly. And this, as Ambrose and Bede say, they do not out of cruelty, but to train them for hunting, lest they grow lax through idleness and neglect to seek their food. So too subordinates too must be driven by their superior to good exercise, and cast from the nest of ease, lest they grow sluggish through idleness.

div.head: Obedience
div.p: Camels teach us obedience. Which, as Isidore says, took their name from the Greek, because, when they are loaded, they bend down before men, humbling themselves, and kneel down upon their knees. For 'camelus' in Greek means 'humble,' or 'short' in Latin: for they are burden-bearing animals, gentle in carrying loads. So too the obedient man ought humbly to take up the burden placed upon him by his superior, and bear it patiently.

div.head: Hatred
div.p: Hatred is the height of envy, just like the serpent called the seps, which, though small, according to Solinus, if it strikes someone, its venom consumes flesh and bone together. Whence Lucan: the wasting seps, dissolving both bone and body together. So too hatred, and so on.

div.head: Offering Oneself to God
div.p: A man ought to offer himself to God, just as, in the Law of Moses, the turtledove and the doves were offered, as is seen in the purification of a woman after childbirth, in Leviticus 12, where a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons were offered. By the turtledove, a solitary bird, is understood the contemplative life, which ought to be offered doubly, according to its double eye: one, by which it contemplates heavenly things, to desire them; the other, by which it looks upon temporal things, to despise them. By the dove is understood the active life, which is offered doubly on account of its double act: for it must be exercised toward oneself, in self-correction, and toward one's neighbor, in his edification or aid.

Likewise, after the manner of the animals that were offered under the Law. Of which a threefold difference is found: one kind was wholly burned, whence it is called a 'holocaust,' as if wholly consumed by fire, signifying that a man ought to offer himself wholly in the fire of divine love, not only in the fulfillment of the commandments, but also of the counsels. Another was offered for sin, which was divided into two parts: one was burned, the other went for the use of the priests, to signify that the expiation of sins comes from God through the ministry of priests, when it was offered for the sin of the whole people; but if it was offered specially for the sin of a priest, then it was wholly burned, for it was not fitting that what was offered for their own sin should come to the use of the priests. The third was called the peace-offering, which was offered for the giving of thanks or for the welfare of those offering it. The first is for the perfect, the second for penitents, the third for those making progress. This third offering was divided into three parts: one part was burned in honor of the one God, another went to the use of the priests, the third to the use of those offering it, to signify that the salvation of man proceeds from God, through the mediation of ministers and the cooperation of the men themselves who are saved.

div.head: Casting Off Occasions of Sin
