div.p: Occasions of sins and temptations must be cast off, after the example of the elephant. Which, as Solinus says, when pressed by the hunt, breaks off both its tusks equally, so that, its ivory forfeited, it will no longer be sought. So too the Lord taught us to cast off even what is dearest to the body, lest we be condemned and our soul be endangered. Matthew 5: if your eye scandalizes you, pluck it out, and so on.

div.head: Diligently and Fully Completing the Church Office at Each Hour
div.p: The wild ass teaches us to perform the Church office diligently and completely at each hour. Which, as Isidore and Jorach say, on the fourth day of March brays twelve times in the night and twelve times in the day, and by its braying at each hour, the number of the hours is known.

div.head: A Work That Ought to Be Done Only Once
div.p: The elephant teaches us that a work which ought to be done only once should be done with much deliberation. Which, according to Aristotle, lives two or three hundred years, and, according to Solinus, gives birth only once in its whole life, carrying its offspring for two years. So too a man ought long to carry, through deliberation of mind, the good deed that he wishes to do only once. Seneca: what is to be decided once must be deliberated long. Pliny, in a certain book: a hen, on the day she lays an egg, will not die from the sting of an asp. So too, on that day when a man does a good work, he will not perish through the temptation of the devil.

div.head: Women's Adornment
div.p: Women's adornment is like the serpent called the situla. Of which Isidore says that it is a small and malicious serpent, which kills a man through thirst. It gleams with such beauty upon its back that it delays those who gaze upon it, holding them in wonder; and, since it is slow, it holds fast, dazed by its marvel, those it cannot otherwise pursue. So too a woman draws the hearts of onlookers to herself by adornment and beauty, and destroys them with the venom of evil consent or deed.
Likewise, she is like the cat, which boasts so much of its beautiful fur that it is caught and skinned; so too a woman boasts so much of her beauty that she is caught by the devil, and so on.

div.head: The Poor
div.p: The poor are despised in this world, but honored in the next, just as a live hen is despised and cast out of the house, while the hawk is honored and set upon a perch or the hand; but the dead hawk is thrown away, while the dead hen will be honored, carried to the table of lords, and so on.

div.head: Punishing and Casting Out the Disruptive
div.p: Bees teach that those who disturb the community must be punished and cast out. Which, as Aristotle says in Book VIII, strike mortally, or drive entirely away from themselves, those who break the peace and wish to steal their honey. To the Galatians 5: would that they were cut off, who trouble you, and so on.

div.head: The Sinner
div.p: The sinner is likened to the mole. Which, as Isidore says, is so named because it is condemned to perpetual blindness, always digging in the earth and turning up the soil. So too the sinner is blind to divine things, always busy and anxious about earthly ones. For, as Aristotle says in a certain book, and Pliny in Book XI, the mole has no sight, though it has the likeness of eyes.
Likewise, as Jorach says, when it is drawn out of the earth and comes into the light of the sun and into the air, it dies. So too the sinner, and so on.

Likewise, they are likened to crows. First, because, as the book On the Natures of Things says, it is a noisy bird, knowing how to say nothing but 'cras, cras' — tomorrow, tomorrow — though it forms various sounds. This fits the proud, who put off their conversion, and noisily cry out against and revile others. Second, because they are cunning, stealthily seizing and hiding things away — this fits the avaricious. Third, because they are unclean, perching on carcasses, and seeking their food in filth and dung — which fits the lustful.

Likewise, they are likened to the bat. For, as Isidore says, the bat is so named because, fleeing the light, it flies about at evening twilight, signifying the lustful, who seek out hiding places and darkness. Job 24: the eye of the adulterer watches for the darkness.

Likewise, he is likened to a certain beast called the manticore. For, as Solinus says in chapter 58, the manticore is born in India, with a triple row of teeth, a human face, gray-blue eyes, a blood-red color, a lion's body, and a tail spiked like a scorpion's sting, with a hiss so shrill that it imitates the melodies of pipes and trumpets sounding together; it craves human flesh most eagerly, and is of great speed. Pliny says the same thing in Book X, as does Avicenna. Its human likeness shows the sin of avarice, since man alone, out of avarice, hoards up money; the lion's likeness, the sin of pride; its blood-red, fiery color, the sin of wrath; the multitude of its teeth is referred to the sin of gluttony; and the scorpion's tail to the sin of slander and envy, whence it also desires above all to devour men by slandering them.

Likewise, he is likened to the mule. First, by reason of unnaturalness. For the mule is generated, contrary to the usual course of nature, from two species — the ass and the mare, the mare thus being subjected to the ass; so too, in sin, the order of nature is perverted, when reason is subjected to sensuality, over which reason ought to rule. Ecclesiasticus 10: I have seen servants upon horses.

Second, by reason of sterility, or nature withholding its benefit from it, since a kind of wrong against nature is, as it were, produced in it. Or, as Aristotle says, it is sterile on account of coldness; so too sin is sterile of meritorious work, on account of the lack of charity.

Third, by reason of turning in circles. For, as Isidore says, the mule is so named from its manner of walking, because it turns the millstone in a circle; so too the sinner, when he is drawn from one sin into another, is, as it were, whirled round in a circle. The Psalmist: the wicked walk about in a circle.

Likewise, he is likened to the salamander. Which, as Pliny says in a certain book, is a venomous animal, that infects the fruit of trees, corrupts the waters, and, if its saliva touches only a man's foot, corrupts his whole body; so too sin is the worst venom, which corrupts the fruit of good works and the waters of grace, and, if its saliva — that is, delight — touches the foot — that is, the affection — it destroys the whole man.

Likewise, he is likened to venom. For 'venenum' is so called because it travels through the veins to the heart; so too sin travels through the veins of thought and delight to the consent of the heart, or, through the bodily senses, as through veins, steals into the arteries of the mind. Jeremiah 9: death has climbed in through our window, and so on.

Likewise, he is likened to the basilisk, or regulus. Which, as Avicenna says, kills by sight and hearing alone. And, as Pliny says in Book VIII, the basilisk has such power that all who see its eyes die at once; it kills not only shrubs it touches, but those it merely breathes upon; it scorches the grass, and shatters rocks. And, as Avicenna says, when a bird flies over its lair, it falls dead. Yet, as Solinus says, it is overcome by the weasel. Likewise, sin kills the mind of man through the scent of lingering delight, or the sight of consent, even if far from the deed; but the remedy against it is the weasel stuffed with rue — that is, penance, full of bitterness, which extinguishes sin.

Likewise, he is likened to the aspis, which, as Isidore says, stops up its ear at the voice of the enchanter — pressing one ear to the ground, and stopping and covering the other with its tail, so as not to hear. So too the sinner stops up one ear with love of earthly things, and the other with the deception of falsehood, so as not to hear what could convert him. The Psalmist: like the asp that is deaf and stops her ears.

Likewise, sin, as long as it is retained, grows and multiplies, after the example of the crocodile, whose length is seventeen cubits, and which, as some say, continues growing as long as it lives. So too sin, unless it is washed away by penance, soon draws another into itself by its own weight.

Likewise, sin abounds more in prosperity than in adversity, just as serpents abound more in summer, and do more harm, than in winter, and more by day than by night, since they are all of a cold nature; and their venom does more harm when they are warmed, whence, being cold, they curl up when touched by the night dew and in winter, but by day and in summer they uncoil themselves to do harm. So too the sinner, like venom, touches the heart, and by his coldness extinguishes the warmth of charity, when he touches the heart through consent — and this more in prosperity, because in its warmth sin grows stronger still. The Psalmist: I will fear because of the terror of the day.

div.head: Penance
div.p: Penance is likened to the phoenix. Which, as Isidore says, living five hundred years and more, when it sees that it has grown old, builds itself a pyre of gathered spice-branches, and, turning to the ray of the sun, with the beating of its wings kindles for itself a fire and a blaze, and so, within three days, rises again from the ashes. Ambrose relates the same thing, in Book V of the Hexameron; Pliny agrees, in Book X, and Solinus, in chapter 33. So too the sinner, when he has long lived in sins, ought, from consideration of divine justice, fear of hell, and the uncertainty of death, to build himself a nest, in which, through the fervor of compunction, through humility, he must be reduced to ashes; and so, after the three days of penance — namely, contrition, confession, and satisfaction — he will rise again, made new.

Likewise, it frees from temptations, as it frees from the deceptions of the merganser, which, when birds of prey pursue it, takes refuge in the water, and is saved by the benefit of submersion; so too the tempted soul ought to plunge itself into the tears of penance, in order to escape.

Likewise, tearful penance makes God overlook sins. For, as Pliny says in a certain book, when the lion perceives, by scent, that the lioness has mated with a leopard, he rises up entirely to punish the adultery; and so the lioness is washed clean of the fault in a river. So too the Lion of the tribe of Judah spares the soul that has washed away its sin in the fountain of tears.

Likewise, it is likened to the panther. Which, as the Physiologus says, has only the dragon as its enemy; having eaten, it hides itself in a cave and sometimes sleeps for three days; then, rising, it sends forth a great cry with a most sweet odor, as of every kind of spice, and all the beasts, near and far, hearing it, flock to that scent and follow it wherever it goes; only the dragon, hearing it and unable to bear it, flees and grows numb, motionless. So too the sinner, after the three days of penance, sends forth the voice of divine praise, and, from his mouth, the sweetest odor of prayer, and all the animals — that is, the virtues — follow him; only the dragon — that is, the demon — flees, together with his sin.

Likewise, it is likened to a certain small creature called the leochophonos. Which, as Pliny says in Book VIII, the lion flees, and which, if it tastes it, has such power in it that it at once kills the king of the four-footed beasts. And so its ashes, flesh, or meal, scattered on the paths of lions and taken up by them, kill them. This little beast, then, represents the humble penitent, whom lions and demons fear and flee; whence such a man, reduced to ashes in contrition, and placed on the paths where demons approach through temptations, kills and puts them to flight.

Likewise, it is likened to a certain stone, which, as Pliny says in a certain book, hinds, when they feel themselves burdened, eat, and it helps them; and after they die, it is found in their belly, and this stone, in a wondrous way, helps pregnant women. So too the soul, feeling itself burdened by sin, ought to take up a hard and harsh penance, which not only frees it in this life from the weight of sins, but after death its power is found freeing from the bitterness of punishments, and it also helps those with child to bring their good purpose and resolve to fulfillment.
Likewise, bitter penance extinguishes the gnawings of conscience, just as wormwood extinguishes fleas; for wormwood is their poison, according to Constantine.

div.head: Penitents Change Their Character
div.p: Penitents, by the power of penance, change their character, and so are likened to certain animals, of which Ambrose says: the lion on land is terrible, but in the sea it is a gentle fish. So too bitter penance turns a fierce man into one gentle and mild. Likewise, according to the same author, the weasel's scent is heavy on land, but sweet in the water — signifying that those who stink through ill repute become fragrant through grace. Likewise, the hare is a timid animal on land, but formidable in the sea, because the washing of penance makes fainthearted and fearful men most strong. Likewise, the wolf on land is a ravenous animal, but in the water a powerless one. Whence he says: these wolves do not know how to make the sheep afraid; so too, through penance, men who were terrible and rapacious become gentle and merciful. Likewise, the pig is an unclean animal on land, but in the sea clean, even for the Jews, who nevertheless do not eat land-pigs — signifying that through the water of penance the uncleanness of life is purged away for them. Likewise, the scorpion on land strikes from behind, but the sea-scorpion does not — instead it restores; so too, through penance, backbiting slanderers are changed into benefactors.

Likewise, penitents are likened to the quail. Which, as the book On the Natures of Things says, crossing the sea, when it grows weary, descends into the water, and, because it fears the hawk, does not rise from there as long as it sees it. So too the sinner, crossing the sea of this world, seeing himself weary with the weight of sin, descends into the water of penance, and, holding one wing close to himself — that is, in penance — but raising the other, that is, the spirit, upward, thus passes through as if sailing. For he ought so to fear on account of justice that he still presumes on mercy; and such a man ought especially to fear the hawk — that is, the devil — and therefore to hold himself close to the earth against him, that is, in humility. For humility alone, as blessed Anthony says, assails the snares of the devil.

Likewise, he is likened to the stork. Which, as the book On the Natures of Things says, when it feels itself weighed down, injects seawater into itself with its beak, through the rear, and so purges itself; whence, in imitation of them, it is said that Galen invented the enema. So too the penitent, weighed down by sin, ought to purge himself with the bitter tears of penance.

Likewise, penitents ought to look to the examples of their betters, and always hide their own works in humility, after the example of the ostrich. Which, as the Physiologus says, does not lay eggs except when the Pleiades rise; then it first lifts its eyes to the Pleiades, then digs a pit in the sand, where it lays its eggs and covers them with sand; and, since it is a forgetful animal, it forgets where it laid them, and never returns to them, nor seeks them further. But the sand, warmed, brings the eggs to hatch by the heat of the sun, and produces the chicks from them, which, once hatched, the mother gathers again and recognizes as her own. Penitents, then, ought to look to the examples of their betters, as the ostrich looks to the Pleiades, and then hide their eggs — that is, their works — in the sand of hard penance, that is, guard them in humility, and never look on them with pride or for display; and then, penance growing warm, the heat of the sun — that is, the love of God — kindles it and brings forth the offspring from it, which the mother who brought them forth — that is, the soul of the penitent — will recognize the more clearly, and gather together, glorious, as her own fruits.

Likewise, he is likened to the tiger, which, according to Isidore, is an animal marked with various spots. Of which Pliny says, in Book VIII, that when its cubs are stolen, it pursues the thief by scent, who, fleeing on the swiftest horse, throws mirrors behind him on the way; the tiger, seeing these and gazing at its own reflection, believing it to be its young, wishes to take it up, and meanwhile the hunter escapes. The swiftly running tiger is the sinner who repents swiftly and fervently, pursuing his 'stolen cubs' when he strives to recover, through penance, the good works lost through sin; and the hunter throws before him mirrors, by which he is detained, because the devil sets before him various obstacles, by which he is hindered.

Likewise, he is likened to the lion. Which, as Aristotle says in Book IX, is born very small, so that at two months it can scarcely walk; afterward it grows and becomes most fierce. So too penitents, at the beginning, are small in virtue, but afterward, growing through charity, are strengthened and become most bold.

Likewise, they are likened to stags, which, as Pliny says in Book XXVIII, are enemies of serpents, whom they draw out of their caverns with the breath of their nostrils and devour; so too the sinner ought, with the breath of discernment, to draw sins out of the caverns of consciences, and so on.

Likewise, as Isidore says, stags, by grazing on dittany, shake out arrows lodged in them. For by dittany, an herb having the power to dissolve, consume, and draw out, is understood penance, which drives out the venom and the arrow of sin.

div.head: Receiving and Helping Pilgrims and Travelers
div.p: Kites teach us to receive and help pilgrims and travelers. Which, as Isidore says, take cuckoos upon their shoulders, on account of their short and feeble flights, lest, wearied by the long stretches of air, they fail along the way. How much more, then, ought man to bear man, according to that verse: 'Bear one another's burdens,' and so on.
Likewise, elephants, which, as Solinus says in chapter 33, if they see a man wandering lost in the desert, lead him to familiar paths.
Likewise, Aristotle says that on a certain mountain guests are not harmed by scorpions, but only the natives are harmed and killed.

div.head: Perfect Men, Likened to Fish
div.p: Perfect men are like fish. Among which the better are those that dwell in the deep waters, on which account, among sea-creatures, the better are those that dwell in the open sea. Likewise, those that dwell in open waters, where the winds freely blow, are better than others that lack this. Likewise, better still are those that dwell in the most vigorously agitated waters. So too perfect men are the better, the higher they are through contemplation, the more open through simple conduct, and the more stirred through good works.

Likewise, they are like birds of prey, of which Aristotle says in Book II that they are the highest and swiftest in flight, and of the greatest boldness, as is clear in the eagle and the falcons; so too these men are high through their conduct. To the Philippians 3: our citizenship is in heaven. Swiftest through love, for, according to Gregory, he who loves more ardently runs more swiftly. Bold through the strength of confidence. Proverbs 28: the just, like a confident lion, shall be without dread.

Likewise, they are likened to the heron. Which, according to Isidore, is so named as if 'ardua' — lofty — on account of its high flights. For it dreads rainstorms, and flies above the clouds, to escape the tempests of rain. So too holy men lift themselves into high and heavenly things, against the storms and temptations of demons. Second, because, although it feeds in the waters, it nests in the woods, in tall trees; so too holy men, though they feed on passing things, ought nonetheless to place the nest of their rest in the highest places.

div.head: Perseverance
div.p: Bees teach perseverance. Which, as Aristotle says in Book VIII, when they go out, do not turn to various flowers, nor leave one flower for another, until they find in it what they seek; so too a man ought not to busy himself in various pursuits, because, according to Gregory, the mind is found weaker in each single thing, the more it is divided, confused, among many.

Likewise, a man ought to persevere in the good that he has heard, for, according to Aristotle, among all animals that have ears, one alone has them immovable, as Aristotle says in Book I, as a sign that one ought to persist in the teaching one has heard.

div.head: Preachers, Likened to Birds of Prey
div.p: Preachers ought to be like birds of prey. Which, as Aristotle says in a certain book, have a curved and sharp beak, so as to hold their prey more firmly and tear the flesh more easily. They are also of little flesh and much feathering, so that their flight may be swifter; they have a thin, long tail, by which, in flying, they steer themselves as if by a rudder. So too the preacher ought to have a mouth turned back upon himself, so that he may first correct his own faults, and himself fulfill what he tells others; and sharp, to cut into and strike hearts; he ought to have little flesh, caring little for the flesh, and abound in the feathers of the virtues.
Likewise, a swift flight — that is, prompt obedience or love. He ought also to have a long tail of prudence, which, according to Boethius, measures the outcomes of things.

Likewise, he is likened to the cock. Which, as Ambrose says, the lion greatly fears, especially the white cock, which some say is on account of the alectorius stone it carries in its belly. So too the devil fears the 'white' preacher — that is, the clean one — on account of Christ, whom he carries in his heart.

Likewise, they are likened to water-birds, which have broad beaks, so as to pull up more easily the grasses and roots of sins from men's hearts. Likewise long necks, so as to draw their food more easily from the depth of the water, by which is signified that they ought to draw the words of Scripture from the depths, and, on account of the length of the neck, meditate at greater length on what is to be spoken, because the vocal breath does not come out at once from a long neck, but, on account of the length of the windpipe, lingers there longer.

Likewise, he is likened to the dog. First, because, as Solinus says in chapter 21, all dogs love their masters, which he proves by many examples. For in Epirus, a dog, recognizing among a crowd the killer of its master, betrayed him by barking; when Jason of Lycia was killed, his dog, refusing food, died of starvation; the dog of King Lysimachus threw itself into the flames, and was burned together with him; two hundred dogs led back the king of the Garamantes from exile, fighting against those who resisted. A certain man condemned at Rome was followed to the prison by his dog with howling, and, once he was killed, the dog, given bread, carried it to the mouth of the deceased, and, when the corpse was thrown into the Tiber, swam alongside it, trying to hold it up. So too preachers ought to love Christ, defend him, follow him in tribulations, and expose themselves to death for him.

Second, because, as Pliny says in Book VIII, dogs alone recognize the voice of their household, and no creature except man has a greater memory; it seeks out tracks, drawing along with it, on a leash, the one who tracks the wild beast, and, though crossing water, catches the wind and scent, and stretches its muzzle toward hidden dens. So too the preacher ought to recognize Christ and hold him continually in memory, catch his prey through the conversion of sinners, always driven by the staff of the divine spirit, and, by the scent and desire of eternal salvation, pursue those living like beasts, exposing vices as though hidden dens in which they seek to hide.

Third, by reason of boldness. For, as Solinus says in the same place, when Alexander sought India, the king of Albania sent him two dogs, one of which spurned the pigs and bears offered to it, offended by such unworthy prey — which Alexander, in his ignorance, ordered destroyed as useless — while the other killed a lion, and, on seeing an elephant, wore down the beast with a fierce bite, and then, to the great astonishment of the onlookers, pinned it to the ground. So too preachers sometimes rebuke great tyrants, as John the Baptist rebuked Herod.

Likewise, he is likened to the beaver. Which, as Isidore says, lives with the four-footed creatures on land, and stays with the swimming creatures in the water. So too the preacher, through the active life, ought to conduct himself like a four-footed creature moving about on land, and, through contemplation, to dwell in the waters of the Scriptures.

Likewise, he ought to be like the bear. Which, as Solinus says in chapter 24, brings forth shapeless offspring, giving birth to tiny scraps of flesh, white in color, without eyes, and shapes them gradually by licking. So too the preacher, if he finds the children whom he bears to God to be carnal and shapeless, ought to shape them, in his spirit, by the teaching of his mouth. To the Galatians 4: my little children, of whom I am again in labor, until... Christ.

div.head: The Prelate
div.p: A prelate ought to be likened to the whale. Which, as Jorach says, loves its young with a wondrous love, and carries them about with itself in the sea for a long time, and if they should be hindered by heaps of sand, it gathers a great quantity of water in its mouth and pours it over them, and so, freeing them from danger, leads them back to the open sea; it exposes itself to every danger for their sake, and when a storm grows strong, it takes them into its belly, and releases them once calm has returned. So too a prelate ought to love his subjects as his children, and lead them with much care through the sea of this world, freeing those caught in the sands of riches with the water of teaching, and set himself before them, and, in adversity, take them into his innermost being, and so on.

Likewise, he is likened to the ram, which is the leader of the flock and the strongest, whence, according to Isidore, it is named from strength, because the ram is the more powerful of the flock among the other sheep; for 'aries' is said to be named from the altars, as is clear in the Law of Moses. So too a prelate ought to be the leader of the flock — presiding by authority, going before by the example of a good life, defending it as the stronger, and offering himself for the flock to the Lord.

Likewise, he ought to be likened to the lion. Which, as Pliny says in a certain book, is said to bring forth shapeless cubs, tiny scraps of flesh the size of weasels at first, scarcely able to walk at six months, scarcely able to move at two months. But the Physiologus says: the lioness gives birth to her cubs dead, and guards them for three days, until their father comes and breathes upon their faces, that they may be brought to life. But according to Isidore, the newborn cubs are said to sleep for three days and two nights, which their father's roaring is said to rouse. So too a prelate, by the roar of preaching and prayer, ought to rouse children dead in their sins. Yet a prelate ought to speak gently to the good. Judges 9: behold, a swarm of bees in the mouth of the lion. For the bee stings, yet makes honey. So too a prelate ought to sting the slow-witted and sweeten the good.

div.head: Progress in Virtue
div.p: A man ought to make progress and grow in the virtues throughout the whole time of the present life, after the example of the stag, whose antlers do not branch out until the age of seven years, since, up to seven years, one branch is added each year, whence their age is discerned by their antlers. For since seven is the universal number, the present age runs its course accordingly, as is clear in the seven days of the week, and so on.

div.head: The Prosperity of the Rich and of Sinners
div.p: The prosperity of the rich and of sinners is likened to the owl. For the owl, as Isidore says, is a bird laden with feathers, held down by heavy sloth, weak in flight, dwelling among the tombs of the dead by day and by night, and is said to portend evil and the desolation of the place it inhabits. So too the rich man, laden with riches, is sluggish toward good works, weak in contemplation, dwells among the corpses of sins, and portends the sign of future desolation — that is, of eternal damnation.

div.head: Prudence
div.p: A man ought to be prudent, like the vulture. Which, as Aristotle says in a certain book, hunts from noon until night, and rests from sunrise until noon. So too a man ought to devote himself partly to the rest of prayer and contemplation, and partly to the provision of necessities.

Likewise, he ought to be likened to the hedgehog. Which, as Isidore says, is a spiny animal, that, as soon as it senses something harmful, curls into a ball and gathers itself into its own weapons, and is so defended by its spiny covering that it can scarcely be touched at all. So too a man ought to wrap himself in the thorns of penance. The Psalmist: when they troubled me, I put on sackcloth, and so on.

Second, because, according to Ambrose, in its den it makes for itself two ways of looking out, one by which it flees the north wind, the other by which it flees the south; so too a man ought to have a way to flee, both in time of adversity and in time of prosperity.

Likewise, after the example of the ant. Which, as Isidore says, provides in summer what it will live on in winter, chooses wheat at harvest-time, and does not touch barley, and when rain falls upon the wheat, it exposes it to the sun.

Likewise, as Pliny says in a certain book, having gathered the grains, it hides them within, so that they may not be seized by birds. So too, first, a man ought to provide, in life, for the time of death. Second, he ought to gather wheat — that is, Christ and eternal things — and not to care for barley — that is, temporal things. Third, if some temptation assails us, we ought to expose it to the sun, that we may be reshaped by the warmth of his charity. Fourth, a man ought to hide his good works, lest they be seized by birds — that is, by demons — through vainglory.

Likewise, like the serpent. Which, as the Physiologus and the book On the Natures of Things say, when it grows old, wastes away its flesh by fasting, until, its skin loosened through leanness, it passes through a crack in a rock, sheds its old skin, and puts on youth; it sheds the skin from the head first. So too we ought to renew our life through works of penance, first by fasting, not only from food, but still more from vices, and so, in the narrow crack of the strait way of life, put off our old garments and take up new life.

Likewise, the brute beasts teach us prudence, as Augustine says in Book XI of the Trinity, in the rearing of their young, in the building of their dens and their forethought for provisions, in their foreknowledge of the change of seasons, and in their love for their own kind.

div.head: Fighting against the Devil
div.p: One must fight against the devil, just as fish fight against the crocodile. For when the crocodile fights against the whale, the fish flee to the whale's tail, and it fights on behalf of itself and them; and since the crocodile cannot win, it sends forth a most foul smoke into the water, against which the whale, sending forth a fragrant smoke from its mouth, drives back that foul odor. So too the crocodile — that is, the devil — attacks someone up to the tail of the whale — that is, up to the utmost point of the life of Christ, namely the example of the Cross and Passion of Christ — and then, by his good odor, every stench of carnal corruption, which the devil has sent forth, will be extinguished...

div.head: The Religious Life
div.p: One entering religious life ought to enter that which best suits his condition, after the example of birds, which, according to their different constitutions, seek different dwellings: for cold and moist birds, such as water-birds, dwell in marshes and rivers, while birds of a hotter nature dwell in mountainous places; so too the weaker, in lower places, and the stronger, in higher ones.

Likewise, those living in community are likened to cranes, which go together, eat together, love their own kind, appoint themselves a king and leader, fly in order and together, and do not stray from the company; by observing this order, they lighten every labor, so that they are relieved in turn by the office of their leader. For one goes ahead, for an appointed time, then turns back and yields the task of leading the flock to the one following. They keep watch by turns; if they quarrel among themselves, they are soon reconciled; they foreknow a coming storm. This is what Ambrose and Basil say, in the Hexameron.

Likewise Isidore. And Solinus, in chapter 10, adds: they divide the watches of the night, so that the tenth crane stays sleepless; the wakeful ones hold small stones in their claws, which, if they should happen to fall, would betray their sleep; they signal by a cry what is to be guarded against. In their social life they teach that solitary singularity is to be avoided in the religious life, and community is to be pursued. In this, that they appoint themselves a king, they teach that obedience is to be observed; and in the alternation of leadership and of watches, they teach that mutual labors are to be shared in turn. And in this, that the wakeful one holds a small stone, it is shown that the one presiding — like Christ, who is the cornerstone — ought always to keep it at the foot of his affection, and preside over others without the sluggishness of negligence, and diligently signal what is to be guarded against. In the book On the Natures of Things it is said that the leader-crane first lowers itself to the ground, and is first to rise from the ground, and raises its head above the rest to look around. So too a prelate, although greater in dignity, ought nevertheless first to lower himself in humility, be the first to rise from the earth with the eagerness of prayer and contemplation, or in fleeing earthly desire, and look around, keeping watch with diligence, and so on.

Likewise, bees teach this. For, as Ambrose says in the Hexameron, bees seem to tend a kind of commonwealth. For they alone, before all living creatures, have offspring in common, dwell in one home, and share a common labor, common food, common flight, and common produce.

div.head: Spiritual Renewal
div.p: The soul is renewed spiritually, like the eagle. The Psalmist: your youth shall be renewed like the eagle's. For Jorach says that the eagle, when its feathers grow old and its sight is dimmed, three times flies up and sharpens its sight and its wings against the sun, and as many times, descending, plunges itself into a spring, and so, after three times, its sight returns, and its feathers, and it sharpens its beak against a rock. So too the soul, grown old and blinded through sin, if it ever rises up from earthly actions and lifts itself higher within itself, considering the state of its own mind, directing itself against the sun of Christ, so that it may be set aflame by his heat, by his love — then it will descend and cast itself into the fountain of tears, and will be renewed, and the oldness of its sins purged, and the sight of its spiritual eyes sharpened, and its beak, once bent toward earthly things, will be directed toward the heavenly.

Likewise, it ought to be renewed like the hawk, whose custom it is, according to Gregory, that when it has old feathers, as the south wind blows, it spreads its wings, so that its limbs may grow warm enough to loosen the old feather; but when the wind fails, spreading and beating its wings against the ray of the sun, it makes for itself a warm breeze, and so, its pores opened, the old feathers fall out and new ones grow. Domesticated hawks, however, so that they may molt better, seek out sheltered and warm places. So too, for the renewal of the soul, the south wind avails — that is, the inspiration of divine grace — or the warmth of the sun — that is, the fervor of penance.
See above, in the chapter on Prudence, on the renewal of the serpent...

div.head: The King, Likened to Bees
div.p: Ambrose, in the Hexameron: the king of bees is formed by nature with clear marks of distinction, so that he excels in size of body and in spirit, and, what is chiefly fitting in a king, in gentleness of character. For though he has a sting, he does not use it for vengeance.

Likewise, he is likened to the lion. Of which Aristotle says, in a certain book, that it is a bold, strong, generous, noble, magnanimous animal, for, according to Isidore, 'leo' in Greek is interpreted 'rex' — king — in Latin.

Likewise, they say lions are merciful, for Pliny says, in Book VIII: there are many signs of the lion's clemency — after raging against men, it turns against women; it kills infants only in great hunger; it spares those who prostrate themselves as suppliants, and, as Isidore says, allows captives it meets to return home. So too a king, and so on.

Likewise, by reason of boldness, as the same Pliny says, in Book VIII, that with whatever great force of hunting dogs, it withdraws contemptuously in the open fields, where it can be seen, but among the thickets and woods it goes at the swiftest run, as if counting concealment a disgrace; in pursuing, it uses a leap, not in flight.

Likewise, he is likened to the eagle, by reason of generosity. For, as Jorach says, the eagle is a great and royal bird which, as the book On the Natures of Things says, divides its prey among the other birds, and allows them to eat it with it. Aristotle, in the Secret of Secrets: it is written in the book of the Asclepiads that the king is praiseworthy and worthy of love who is likened to the eagle ruling among the birds, and not the one who is likened to one of the subject birds.

div.head: The Blood of Christ
div.p: The blood of Christ. In the book On the Natures of Things it is said, in chapter 4: King Solomon, wishing to cut hard marble for the altar without iron, shut up the chick of an ostrich in a glass vessel; and when the mother could not free it, seeing this, the ostrich ran to the desert and brought back a little worm, with whose blood it smeared the glass, and the glass shattered, and so it freed its chick. Seeing this, Solomon used a worm of that kind for cutting the hardest marble. And so that worm, which is called the 'tamur,' is named from the effect of Solomon's worm. If the blood of a worm could do this, how much more does the blood of Christ soften and cleave the hardest, adamantine hearts of men.

Likewise, in the book On the Natures of Things: elephants are captured in this way: two virgin girls go into the wilderness, one of whom carries an urn, the other a sword, and sing with loud voices; hearing this, the elephant comes to meet them, and, as if by natural instinct recognizing the innocence of virginal flesh, reveres it with the sweetness of love, and, licking their breasts, is wonderfully delighted and dissolved into sleep. Without delay, the girl with the sword then pierces its belly and pours out its blood, which the other catches in the urn, and with this the royal purple is dyed. This can signify the blood of Christ poured out, which one girl — the Synagogue — cruelly poured out, while the other — the Church — catches in the urn of the chalice. With this blood the royal and nuptial garment is dyed, by which man is prepared for the heavenly feast.

div.head: Holy Men
div.p: Holy men are likened to doves. For, as the Gloss on the Song of Songs says, in the first book, the dove lacks gall, does not wound with its beak, feeds the young of others, remains near flowing streams, chooses the best grains, replies to song with a moan, flies in flocks, defends itself with its wings, and recovers its sight. That it lacks gall attests to simplicity and innocence; that it does not wound with its beak, to kindness and goodwill; that it feeds the young of others, to compassion and mercy; that it remains near streams, to zeal and diligence; that it chooses the best grains, to divine wisdom; its moaning, to penance; its flying in flocks, to holy fellowship.

Likewise, by reason of fruitfulness, for Aristotle says that doves lay eggs and hatch young almost the whole year, but in a warm region they hatch once a month; so too the saints ought to be fruitful in good works throughout the whole time.

Likewise, they are likened to the falcon, or hawk. First, because it has little flesh; so too the saints have little of carnal desires. Second, because it has much boldness. Third, because it has great agility. Fourth, because it has great nobility. Let these be applied.

Likewise, they are likened to lambs. First, by reason of simplicity and innocence. For Ambrose says: the lamb is the simplest among the animals. Whence Isidore says that nature armed all the other animals, and left the lamb alone unarmed.

Second, by reason of gentleness, for Aristotle says, in a certain book: sheep are more peaceable than other animals, and closer to men; this is clear, for it neither wounds with the tooth, nor attacks with the horn, nor tears with the claw, nor strikes with the hoof.

Third, by reason of usefulness, for, as the book On the Natures of Things says, everything in the sheep is useful — wool, hide, flesh, milk; so too holy men, as much as they can, ought to procure the benefit of others.

Fourth, by reason of prudence, for Isidore says: the lamb is named from 'recognizing,' because, among many flocks, it recognizes even its mother by her bleating alone. Likewise, by natural instinct, it recognizes its enemy, the wolf. So too the saints ought to recognize the Church and grace, their mother, who bore them, and the devil, the wolf, who harms them — following the mother, fleeing the devil.
Likewise, they are likened to horses. First, by reason of boldness, of which Job speaks...

Second, by reason of discernment. First, because some recognize no one but their own masters, as Solinus says in chapter 51, that Alexander's horse, called Bucephalus, once he had received the royal saddle, deigned to carry no one but his master. Likewise, the horse of Gaius Caesar received no one but Caesar on its back. So too the saints disdain to carry, in their hearts, anything but their Master, according to that verse: 'You were bought at a great price,' and so on.

Third, by reason of fidelity. For, as Solinus says in the same place, when the king of the Scythians, defeated in single combat, was about to be despoiled by his victorious adversary, he was torn by the kicks and bites of his own horse. Likewise, when King Nicomedes was killed, his horse ended its life by refusing food. So too the saints ought to contend faithfully for Christ, and so on.
Fourth, by reason of devotion, for according to Solinus, in the same place, some horses weep for their masters; so too the saints weep on hearing or reading of the Passion of the Lord.

Likewise, they are likened to lions. First, by reason of boldness — yet, according to Pliny, when pursued, they do not hide, but wish to be seen. So too the saints do not flee their persecutors, but offer themselves to them.

Second, because, as Isidore says, lions, hemmed in by hunters, gaze at the ground, so as to be less terrified by the raised spears; but they watch the hunters, so that, having seen them, they may take fright and be roused all the more. So too the just man, having seen and considered his persecutors, grows stronger in patience.

Third, because, according to Pliny, when it pursues prey, it uses a leap; when pursued, it does not flee, but goes at a slow pace. So too the saint ought to pursue the prize of reward by leaping, but not flee the persecution of tribulation. Though the lion is bold, he says, it nevertheless greatly fears the open road, fire, and the creaking of wheels. So too the saints fear the open road — that is, death — the creaking of wheels — that is, the turning of fortune — and the fire of hell.

Second, by reason of generosity, because it is ashamed to eat its prey alone, and so it often leaves some of its catch to other beasts following at a distance. This, in the saints, corresponds to the giving of alms. Third, by reason of cunning. For, as Isidore says, lions, as they walk, wipe out their tracks with their tail, so that they cannot be found by hunters. So too the saints, by later penance, blot out their earlier sins. The Psalmist: blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered.
Likewise, when they sleep, their eyes keep watch, according to Isidore, for it sleeps with open eyes, so that even sleeping it may foresee dangers. The Song of Songs: I sleep, but my heart watches.
Fourth, by reason of abstinence and frugality. For Pliny says, in Book VIII: lions rarely drink, and feed only every other day. So too holy men ought to be abstinent in food and drink.

Likewise, some saints are like elephants. Which, as Solinus says in a certain chapter, rush upon their enemies with an unbearable charge, and cannot be repelled or delayed, moving in battle like immovable mountains; the roar of their trumpeting disturbs the confidence of all, and yet they most greatly flee the smell of a mouse. So too some saints, who overcome the greatest things, are sometimes terrified by the smallest, as Paul, caught up to the third heaven, and having experienced the dangers of every tribulation, full of virtues, was oppressed by a thorn in the flesh, and, fearing to be relieved of it by his own power, was heard by mercy instead.

Likewise, they are likened to hares. Which, as Isidore says, are called 'lepus' as if 'levipes' — light-footed: for it is a swift-running and quite timid animal; so too the saints are swift to flee evils and pursue what is good, and always fearful, lest they be ensnared in something. Proverbs 28: blessed is the man who is always fearful.

Second, because, as Pliny says in Book XI, hares sleep with their eyes open. So too the inner eyes ought always to be open toward divine things, and to guard against adversity. Third, it has hind legs longer than its front ones, so that it climbs more easily than it descends, and so, when it flees, it runs toward the mountain. So too the saints, fleeing the world, ought to climb the mountain, Christ, and be more fit for ascent, in progress, than for descent, in the failure of good.

Likewise, they are likened to the badger. Of which Pliny says, in a certain book, that when pursued by dogs, it holds its breath, and so swells up its skin, and thus avoids the dogs' bites. So too the holy man, when he suffers persecutions and injuries, through patience restrains his spirit within himself, lest he burst out through impatience or anger, and so escapes their bite, lest they harm his soul.

div.head: Heavenly Wisdom
div.p: None can perceive heavenly wisdom unless clean from the filth of sin, just as bees drink only clear water, and do not drink it unless they first cast out the dregs, as Avicenna says. So too a man will not drink the clear water of wisdom, unless he first casts out from himself the dregs of guilt.

div.head: Knowledge Joined to a Bad Life
div.p: One who has knowledge along with a bad life is like the onocentaur, a monstrous creature composed of man and ass. For from the navel up it has a human form; so too the learned but self-indulgent man is, on one side, rational, and on the other, beastly.

div.head: The Solitary
div.p: Solitaries are likened to roe deer. Which, according to Isidore, dwell on high mountains, and see most keenly.

Likewise, it is very swift in running, and, according to Ambrose, avoids harmful things by scent alone, and, with dittany, expels arrows from a wound. So too these men are lofty through heavenly conduct, see keenly through contemplation, run most swiftly through obedience and good works, avoid harmful things by scent through discernment, and, with dittany — that is, penance — expel the arrows of sins through compunction.

div.head: Avoiding Bad Company
div.p: The hind teaches us to avoid bad company. Which, according to Aristotle in Book VII, wishing to give birth, avoids the paths known to other wild beasts, and gives birth near a road, since animals do not come to that place, because of the men there; so too a man, wishing to bring forth a good resolve, ought to avoid the byways of the wicked.

div.head: The Holy Spirit, Likened to the Dove
div.p: The Holy Spirit is likened to the dove

div.head: Spiritual Men
div.p: ...on account of its properties set out above, in the chapter 'Holy men'; spiritual men are likened to it in the same way. Subjects ought to conduct themselves toward their prelate as bees toward their king: see above, in the chapter 'Good men.'

div.head: The Proud
div.p: The proud are likened to bulls. First, by reason of ferocity. For they are most fierce, although they are said to grow gentle when tied to a fig tree, as Isidore says. So too the proud are fierce in doing harm, unless restrained beneath the fig tree — that is, under the authority of a good man.

Likewise, pride. As the book On the Natures of Things says, the falena is an animal born in remote parts of the world, which, by natural instinct, detests pride in men. For it strives to disfigure the man who attacks it, as the conqueror of pride, but allows the man who flees from it — that is, out of fear of humiliation — to escape by standing still.

Likewise, the mastiff, according to Adelinus, is a cruel beast which, though terrible and fearsome to strong men, and boldly assails them, nevertheless flees children it meets, and their words. So too the devil boldly attacks the strong and proud of this world, but flees children, the innocent and the humble.

Likewise, pride is like the serpent called the pestis. Of which Solinus says that whomever it bites is swollen with an enormous bloating, as if dropsical, and so dies. So too pride sinks under its own swelling, and leads to eternal death.
Second, by reason of solitariness. For Aristotle says, in a certain book: the bull grazes alone, except when the time of mating draws near. The Psalmist: the solitary wild beast has devoured it.

Third, by reason of cruelty. For bulls have a hard and cruel heart, whence, according to Aristotle in a certain book, a hard bone is often found in the heart of a bull, by which is signified the hardness of heart in the proud. Ecclesiasticus 3: a hard heart shall fare ill at the last.

Likewise, he is likened to the dragon. Which, as Pliny says in Book VIII, the dragons of India are so large that with an easy coil they encircle elephants and bind them in a deadly knot, so that when the elephant falls, its weight crushes the coiled dragon; and they are so huge that they drink up all the elephant's blood, and, when the bloodless elephant collapses, it crushes the drunken dragon, and so the victor dies together with the vanquished. So too the proud man lies in wait for one greater who rules, and sometimes for his blood, and thus attacks that 'elephant,' sometimes openly, sometimes secretly, and so falls together with him.

Likewise, he is likened to the buffalo, whose ferocity and strength cannot be tamed, except by an iron ring fastened in its nostrils, as is said in the book On the Natures of Things. So too the presumption of the proud is checked only by tribulation or oppression. Whence in the Second Book of Kings it was said to him: I will put a ring in your nostrils, and so on.

div.head: Escaping the Snares of Temptations
div.p: The mullet fish teaches us to escape the snares of temptations. Which is so named, according to Isidore, because it is very agile: for wherever it perceives the ambushes set by fishermen, it turns back at once and leaps so straight that you would think the fish were flying. So too he who perceives the snares of temptations, as it were, draws back, withdrawing himself from what would destroy him through temptations, and passes by most swiftly, when, right at the beginning of the temptation, he turns himself away from it.
Likewise, the stag teaches this. Which, as hunters say, pursued by dogs, enters the waters, and drinks the waters of wisdom or of tears, and is refreshed, and so on.

Likewise, tempting demons are like animals of prey. For some hunt by night, like some wolves; some by day, like dogs and bears; some by day and by night, like certain other wolves. So too some demons tempt by night — that is, secretly, under the appearance of good, as when one sometimes suggests abstinence, so as to induce impatience; but some tempt by day — that is, openly suggesting some evil, such as murder or lust. Some do both: for they first tempt subtly and secretly, so as to make one fall into open evil.

The untempted man ought to arm himself like the wild boar against hunters, which arms itself in three ways. First, by presenting the harder part of its body; for it has on its flank something like a strong shield, which it turns to face them. Second, by sharpening its tusks — that is, its longer teeth — rubbing them against a tree. Third, by chewing oregano, it sharpens its teeth, as Avicenna says. So too a man ought first to set against the harshness of temptations the harshness — that is, the roughness — of the body. The Psalmist: when they troubled me, I put on sackcloth, I humbled my soul with fasting. Second, to rub his tusks against the tree — that is, to measure his own strength against the virtues of strong and holy men, so that, by their example, he may become stronger in resisting. Third, to chew oregano — that is, the word of God — for the word of God is living and effective, and sharper than any two-edged sword.

Likewise, the devil, tempting, is likened to the bear. Which, as Isidore says, has a weak head, but its greatest strength is in its forelegs and loins; so too temptation is sometimes weak at the beginning, as it were in the head, but becomes very strong in the forelegs — that is, as it advances.

div.head: Those Afraid to Begin Penance
div.p: Those afraid to begin penance are like the ass. Which, as Pliny says in Book VIII, so dreads water that it is careful never to wet even its feet, and drinks from no fountain but a familiar one, so as to go to drink dry-footed, nor does it cross bridges through which the water can be seen shining below. So too he fears to enter the water who fears to enter penance; and he fears to cross the bridge through which the waters shine who fears to enter religious life, whose austerities he sees; and so such men drink from nothing but familiar waters — that is, familiar delights.

div.head: Tyrants
div.p: Tyrants are likened to the eagle. Which, as Aristotle says in Book VIII, casts out its own chicks from every place around it; so too a tyrant does not spare his innocent subjects.
Likewise, they are like kites, which, although birds of prey, do not attack wild birds, but the young of domestic ones; so too tyrants attack only those unable to defend themselves.
Likewise, he is likened to the manticore, of which above, in the chapter on Avarice.
Likewise, they are likened to griffins, of which in the same place.
Likewise, to lions, in cruelty.
Likewise, to wolves — of all of which you will find more above, in the other chapters.

div.head: Tribulation Preserves the Just
div.p: Tribulation preserves the just, after the example of fish, which are better and better preserved in the northern and eastern seas than in the southern, because by the forceful blowing of those winds the waters are more stirred and better purified, on account of which the fish there are more thoroughly cleansed of impurities. By the north wind, then, understand the harshness of adversity; by the east wind, which is warm by its origin, understand the fervor of impending temptation, by which the soul is driven and roused toward the good, and is the more purely preserved. But by the south wind, which is milder and gentler, understand the sweetness of temporal consolation, by which men, like fish living in the water of penance or justice, grow slack, and are therefore less well preserved.

Likewise, severe tribulation compels a man to go to God, just as Pliny says, in a certain book, that the stag, when hard pressed by dogs, flees of its own accord to a man. The Psalmist: fill their faces with shame, and they shall seek your name.

Likewise, he is likened to the oryx. Of which Pliny says, in Book II: Egypt calls the oryx a wild beast which, at the rising of the Dog-star, is said to face it and gaze upon it, as if praying — and this it does after it has slept. The sleeping beast — that is, the sluggish mind of the sinner — is roused by the rising of the Dog-star — that is, of burning tribulation — and is made ready, as it were, for prayer, since it is humbled to penance and devotion, when it is thus wounded by tribulation.

div.head: Vainglory
div.p: Vainglory is likened to the moth. Of which Gregory says, in the fourth book of the Moralia: the moth is born from the garment, and, by being born, corrupts the very garment from which it arises. Likewise, vainglory is born from a good work, and makes the heart itself grow worthless. Second, because, as he says, the moth does damage without making any sound, for it consumes the garment almost imperceptibly. So too with vainglory, for, as Valerius says in a certain book, there is absolutely no humility so great that it is not touched by the sweetness of glory.

Third, because, just as, according to Avicenna in Book IV of the Canon, wormwood, calamint, and citron-peel keep cloth from the moth — as these things keep out the moth, so tribulation keeps out vainglory.

div.head: We Are Born and Nourished by the Word of God
div.p: We are born and nourished by the word of God. For the chick is born from the egg and nourished by the egg, since, according to Aristotle in Book VII, the chick is formed from the white of the egg and nourished by the yolk. But we are born by the Word of God. James 1: of his own will he brought us forth by the word of truth, and we are nourished in it. Matthew: man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God.

div.head: The Widow
div.p: A widow ought to be like the turtledove. Which, as Isidore says, is a chaste bird, dwelling covered in the mountains and deserts, and flees the company of men; in winter, its feathers shed, it is said to hide in the hollows of trees, and comes out in spring. So too widows ought to be chaste, solitary, fleeing harmful and vain spectacles, dwelling in the mountains and deserts of an austere life, hiding, their adornment shed, in the winter of present adversity, and coming forth to God in the time of spring — that is, of heavenly grace. Likewise, like the turtledove, she ought to avoid all that is unclean...

div.head: The Ways of Sinners
div.p: The ways of sinners are like birds. First, because, as Pliny says in Book X, every animal has a certain and consistent manner of gait proper to its kind, but birds alone are carried through the air and over the land by an aimless course. Whence, according to Isidore, birds are so named as if from 'sine via' — without a way. So too sinners, in their actions, stray from the way of reason, and wander indeterminately, now rising through pride, now descending through avarice, now turning to the right through pleasure and lust, now to the left through wrath and impatience, now going backward through faintheartedness or despair.

Second, because, by the motion of their wings, they cleave the air, but soon leave no sign of their passing; so too the prosperity of sinners, once they are shut away and dead, fails utterly. Wisdom 5: all these things have passed away, and so on, up to: like a bird that flies across.

div.head: Preserving Virginity
div.p: Vultures teach us to preserve virginity.

Likewise bees, as in the same place above. Likewise, as Aristotle says in Book VIII, bees do not sting young virgins most of all; this pertains to their gentleness and the graciousness of their company.

Likewise, as Avicenna says, young and virgin bees make better honey; so too the young, and especially virgins, have a sweeter spirit of contemplation, since the more strongly the flesh is subjected to the spirit, the more sweetly is the honey of heavenly sweetness produced. Judges 14: out of the strong came forth sweetness.

div.head: The Moral Virtues
div.p: Swallows teach us the moral virtues. First, temperance in food, for, as Isidore says, it takes its food not while sitting on the ground, but while flying in the air.

Second, prudence, in that it builds its nest so skillfully. So too they teach us to build and purify the nest of the mind, skillfully and prudently, with the virtues. For, as Pliny says in Book X, the young of swallows, with notable cleanliness, cast their droppings outside the nest. So too a man ought to cast the filth of sins out of the nest of his conscience. Likewise, it observes the seasons, for in winter it withdraws to warm regions, and returns in summer; so too, and so on.

Likewise, it teaches fortitude, for Pliny says, in a certain book, that there is a certain kind of swallow which all birds fear, which even the eagle flees, and does not dare make prey of it, because its bite is perhaps venomous. So too the birds — that is, the demons — flee those strong in faith, and so on. Likewise, a multitude of virtues does not weigh down the soul, but rather lightens it for ascending to heaven, just as birds abounding in feathers are lifted upward more quickly and move more swiftly, as is clear in birds of prey.
Likewise, ants teach fortitude and patience, which, according to Solinus, often carry burdens greater than their own bodies.

div.head: The Moral Life of Men, Like the Natural Life of Birds
div.p: The moral life of men is like the natural life of birds. For some birds feed on flesh, like birds of prey, according to Aristotle in a certain book, to which carnal men are likened. Some feed on plants, like water-birds, and to these penitents are likened. Some feed on seeds, to which the perfect and spiritual are likened — for the seed is the word of God. Ambrose, in the Hexameron: birds that feed on flesh have rough claws, a sharp beak, and swift flight, so that they can easily catch the prey they pursue, and, once caught, tear it open with claw or beak. So too carnal men have hooked claws for seizing, sharp beaks for slandering, and swift flight for pursuing.

div.head: The Spiritual Life Needs Fewer Things Than the Bodily Life
div.p: The spiritual life needs fewer things than the bodily life. An example of this appears in the instruments by which an animal is moved. For, as Avicenna says, every creature with noble blood is moved by four instruments — that is, by four feet, or by two feet and two hands, as men, or by two feet and two wings, as birds. But certain bloodless animals have more feet, such as crabs, bees, flies, and so on. So too he has noble blood who has the moisture of grace, which is the seat of the spiritual life; but he is moved either by the four feet of the moral virtues — two of these feet being the two loves, of God and of neighbor — while the two wings are the teaching of the two Testaments, which lift the mind in contemplation, or prayer and fasting, by one of which the soul is raised, by the other the body. The two hands, meanwhile, are good works — whether in prosperity, taken by the right hand, or in adversity, by the left. But other sinners, deprived of grace and the virtues, are occupied with many cares and preoccupations.

div.head: Vices to Be Corrected
div.p: The vices which we must correct are signified by the animals that could be offered in sacrifice under the Law of Moses. For there were offered the calf, the kid, and the lamb. We offer the calf against the pride of the flesh; the lamb, when we correct irrational impulses; and the kid, when we restrain wantonness.

Likewise, by the various birds and animals forbidden as food under the Law, various vices are forbidden: as in the prohibition against eating the eagle, which flies high, pride is forbidden; in the griffin, which is hostile to horses and men, cruelty is forbidden; and so with the rest...

div.head: Voluptuous Pleasure
div.p: Voluptuous pleasure is likened to the amphisbaena serpent. Which, as Pliny says in Book IX, has a double head, one in its proper place, another in its tail, as if it were not enough for venom to pour from one mouth. So too pleasure has two heads: gluttony and lust.

Pleasure is like the slug. Which, as Isidore says, the 'limax' is, as it were, a 'worm of mud' — always filthy, and, wherever it crawls, leaves unclean tracks behind it; so too the man given to pleasure.

div.head: Usury
div.p: Usury is likened to the feathers of the eagle, as Pliny says in Book XVIII, which, when placed together with the feathers of other birds, corrode them, as if thirsting. So too usurious money, joined with other money, infects and corrodes the whole...

div.head: Christ, Likened to the Hen
div.p: Christ likened himself to a hen. Luke 23. For, as the Gloss says, the hen is most devoted toward her chicks, gathers them beneath her wings to defend them against the kite, grows sick for love of her chicks, cares more for her chicks than for herself, and feeds them more than herself; for love of them she grows, as it were, hoarse and changes her voice, sheds her feathers, and, as if grown witless, walks about with her wings drooping. So too Christ gathers his faithful beneath the wings of his protection in one faith, defends them against the kite — that is, the raging world — appeared weak upon the cross for love of them, and fed them with the food of his teaching; he became, as it were, hoarse from the cry of his calling, laid aside his garments when he was scourged, and, as if made altogether foolish, hid his power, his wings of divinity lowered.

Likewise, he is likened to the rhinoceros. Which, as Isidore says, is the unicorn, because it has, in the middle of its forehead, one horn so sharp and strong that whatever it attacks, it tosses and pierces through; yet a virgin is set before it, who, as it comes, opens her lap, in which it, laying aside all its ferocity, lays its head, and so, lulled to sleep, is captured as though unarmed. So too God the Son of God, before the Incarnation, was most fierce, but was made gentle in the lap of a virgin, so that afterward he was captured, bound, and slain. Jorach, in his book On the Animals: the rhinoceros, or unicorn, kills elephants with its horn, and is of such strength that it cannot be captured by hunters; but when it senses the hunter's weapon, it lies down before the lap of a virgin, and so is captured. So too the Son of God, sensing the weapon of love for man, cast himself into the womb of the most blessed Virgin; so too, and so on...

div.head: Jealousy
div.p: The jealousy of the jealous man is likened to the wild ass. Which, as Pliny says in Book VIII, fears rivals in its lust, and so guards its pregnant mates and, biting, castrates the males born to them that it suspects of belonging to another, which the mothers, knowing this, hide from it; so too many men hold their relatives under suspicion regarding their wives. Against this, Ecclesiasticus 8: be not jealous of the wife of your bosom. Here ends the fourth treatise, on animals.
